description: Comprehensive Chemistry question bank derived from General Sciences - Chemistry study material for FDA & SDA competitive examination preparation. Covers Basic Concepts, Atomic Structure, Periodic Table, Chemical Bonding, Chemical Reactions, Acids/Bases/Salts, Metals/Non-metals, Carbon/Organic Chemistry, Chemistry in Everyday Life, and Environmental Chemistry.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is chemistry?

options.B: The branch of science that studies the composition, structure, properties and transformations of matter
options.D: The study of forces and motion

questions.explanation: Chemistry is the branch of science that studies the composition, structure, properties and transformations of matter, including the energy changes involved.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a common physical state of matter?
questions.explanation: The three common physical states of matter are solid, liquid and gas. Plasma is another state found in conditions such as stars and electrical discharges. Energy is not a state of matter.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is matter?

options.A: Anything that has mass and occupies space

questions.explanation: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. Matter is made of atoms, molecules or ions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which state of matter has definite shape and volume?
questions.explanation: Solids generally have definite shape and volume, are difficult to compress, and have particles closely packed with limited movement.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which state of matter has definite volume but no fixed shape?
questions.explanation: Liquids have definite volume but no fixed shape; they flow, take the shape of their container and are only slightly compressible.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which state of matter is highly compressible and expands to fill its container?
questions.explanation: Gases have neither fixed shape nor fixed volume, are highly compressible and expand to fill their container.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is diffusion?

options.A: The settling of particles at the bottom
options.B: The spontaneous mixing of particles due to their random motion
options.C: The change of state from solid to liquid
options.D: The separation of mixtures by filtration

questions.explanation: Diffusion is the spontaneous mixing of particles due to their random motion; it is generally fastest in gases and slower in liquids and solids.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: In which state of matter is diffusion fastest?
questions.explanation: Diffusion is generally fastest in gases and slower in liquids and solids due to the greater freedom of movement of gas particles.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a physical property?

options.A: A property that describes chemical reactivity
options.B: A property that can be observed or measured without changing a substance's chemical identity
options.C: A property that always involves a chemical change
options.D: A property that cannot be measured

questions.explanation: A physical property is a property that can be observed or measured without changing a substance's chemical identity; examples include colour, density, melting point and boiling point.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a chemical property?
questions.explanation: Flammability is a chemical property that describes a substance's ability to undergo a chemical change. Density, melting point, and colour are physical properties.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a physical change?

options.A: A change that produces a new chemical substance
options.B: A change in form, size or state that does not produce a new chemical substance
options.C: A change that always releases heat
options.D: A change that cannot be reversed

questions.explanation: A physical change is a change in form, size or state that does not produce a new chemical substance; examples include melting ice, cutting paper and dissolving sugar in water.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a chemical change?
questions.explanation: Rusting is a chemical change in which one or more new substances with different chemical compositions are formed. Melting ice, cutting paper and dissolving sugar are physical changes.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Is every physical change reversible?

options.A: Yes, all physical changes are reversible
options.B: No, some physical changes such as breaking glass are not easily reversed
options.C: Only changes involving heat are reversible
options.D: Only changes involving water are reversible

questions.explanation: No, many physical changes are reversible, but some, such as breaking glass or cutting paper, are not easily reversed.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a pure substance?

options.A: A mixture of two or more substances
options.B: Matter consisting of a single chemical substance with a definite composition
options.D: A substance that cannot be broken down

questions.explanation: A pure substance is matter consisting of a single chemical substance with a definite composition and characteristic properties; elements and compounds are pure substances.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an element?

options.A: A substance made of two or more different atoms chemically combined
options.B: A pure substance made of atoms having the same number of protons
options.D: A substance that can be decomposed by chemical methods

questions.explanation: An element is a pure substance made of atoms having the same number of protons; it cannot be decomposed into simpler substances by ordinary chemical methods.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a compound?

options.A: A physical combination of elements in variable proportions
options.B: A pure substance formed when two or more different elements chemically combine in fixed proportions
options.C: A substance made of only one type of atom
options.D: A mixture that can be separated by filtration

questions.explanation: A compound is a pure substance formed when two or more different elements chemically combine in fixed proportions by mass; its properties differ from those of its constituent elements.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a mixture?

options.A: A chemical combination of elements in fixed proportions
options.B: A physical combination of two or more substances in variable proportions
options.C: A pure substance with definite composition
options.D: A compound formed by chemical reaction

questions.explanation: A mixture is a physical combination of two or more substances in variable proportions; the components retain their chemical identities and can often be separated physically.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a homogeneous mixture?

options.B: A mixture with uniform composition and properties throughout
options.C: A mixture that settles on standing
options.D: A mixture that can be separated by filtration

questions.explanation: A homogeneous mixture has uniform composition and properties throughout, such as salt solution or air.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a heterogeneous mixture?
questions.explanation: A heterogeneous mixture has a composition that is not uniform throughout, such as oil and water or sand in water. Salt solution, air, and sugar solution are homogeneous mixtures.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a solution?

options.A: A heterogeneous mixture that settles on standing
options.B: A homogeneous mixture of two or more substances
options.D: A compound formed by chemical reaction

questions.explanation: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances; a solution may be solid, liquid or gaseous.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a solute?

options.A: The component that dissolves the other substance
options.B: The substance dissolved in a solvent to form a solution
options.C: The insoluble particles in a suspension
options.D: The gas produced in a reaction

questions.explanation: A solute is the substance dissolved in a solvent to form a solution; it is commonly present in a smaller amount, although this is not an absolute rule.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a solvent?

options.B: The component of a solution that dissolves the solute
options.C: The insoluble solid in a mixture
options.D: The product of a chemical reaction

questions.explanation: A solvent is the component of a solution that dissolves the solute; it is commonly present in the larger amount.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a suspension?

options.A: A homogeneous mixture that does not settle
options.B: A heterogeneous mixture containing relatively large insoluble particles that may settle on standing
options.C: A pure substance with definite composition

questions.explanation: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture containing relatively large insoluble particles that may settle on standing and can generally be separated by filtration.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a colloid?

options.A: A homogeneous mixture that settles on standing
options.B: A mixture in which particles of one substance are dispersed in another and scatter light
options.D: A compound formed by chemical reaction

questions.explanation: A colloid is a mixture in which particles of one substance are dispersed in another; particles do not normally settle on standing and scatter light (Tyndall effect).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the Tyndall effect?

options.A: The settling of particles in a suspension
options.B: The scattering of light by colloidal particles making the path of a beam visible
options.C: The dissolving of a solute in a solvent
options.D: The change of state from liquid to gas

questions.explanation: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of light by colloidal particles, making the path of a beam visible; it helps distinguish many colloids from true solutions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is filtration?

options.A: A separation method based on boiling points
options.B: A separation method in which an insoluble solid is retained by a porous filter
options.C: A method of purifying solids by forming crystals
options.D: A method of separating miscible liquids

questions.explanation: Filtration is a separation method in which an insoluble solid is retained by a porous filter while the fluid passes through.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is distillation?

options.A: A separation method based on differences in boiling points or volatility
options.B: A method of separating insoluble solids
options.C: A method of purifying solids by crystallization
options.D: A method of separating dyes by chromatography

questions.explanation: Distillation is a separation or purification method based on differences in boiling points or volatility; the vapour is condensed and collected.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is fractional distillation?

options.A: A distillation technique using a fractionating column to separate miscible liquids with close boiling points
options.B: A method of separating insoluble solids
options.C: A method of purifying solids by crystallization
options.D: A method of separating dyes by chromatography

questions.explanation: Fractional distillation is a distillation technique using a fractionating column to separate miscible liquids with relatively close boiling points, such as components of petroleum or liquid air.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is evaporation as a separation method?

options.A: Removal of a volatile solvent by vaporisation, leaving a dissolved non-volatile solid behind
options.B: Separation of insoluble solids by filtration
options.C: Purification of solids by forming crystals
options.D: Direct change from solid to gas

questions.explanation: Evaporation is the removal of a volatile solvent by vaporisation, leaving a dissolved non-volatile solid behind; it is used to obtain salt from seawater.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is crystallisation?

options.A: A method of separating insoluble solids
options.B: Purification of a solid by forming crystals from a suitable solution
options.C: A method of separating miscible liquids
options.D: Direct change from solid to gas

questions.explanation: Crystallisation is the purification of a solid by forming crystals from a suitable solution; impurities tend to remain in the mother liquor.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is sublimation?

options.B: Direct change from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state

questions.explanation: Sublimation is the direct change from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state; it can separate sublimable substances such as ammonium chloride or iodine from non-sublimable impurities.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is chromatography?

options.A: A separation technique based on different rates of movement of components between a stationary phase and a mobile phase
options.B: A method of separating insoluble solids
options.C: A method of purifying solids by crystallization
options.D: A method of separating miscible liquids by boiling points

questions.explanation: Chromatography is a separation technique based on different rates of movement of components between a stationary phase and a mobile phase; it is used to separate dyes, pigments and mixtures.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an atom?

options.A: The smallest unit of a compound
options.B: The smallest unit of an element that retains its chemical identity
options.C: A group of molecules bonded together
options.D: A mixture of protons and electrons

questions.explanation: An atom is the smallest unit of an element that retains its chemical identity; it consists of a nucleus and electrons.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a molecule?

options.A: The smallest unit of an element
options.B: A group of two or more atoms chemically bonded together and acting as a distinct entity

questions.explanation: A molecule is a group of two or more atoms chemically bonded together and acting as a distinct entity; examples include H2, O2, and CO2.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is atomic mass?

options.A: The mass of an atom commonly expressed in unified atomic mass units (u)
options.B: The number of protons in an atom
options.C: The number of neutrons in an atom
options.D: The total number of protons and electrons

questions.explanation: Atomic mass is the mass of an atom, commonly expressed in unified atomic mass units (u); 1 u is defined as one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is relative atomic mass (Ar)?

options.A: The mass of an atom in grams
options.B: The weighted mean mass of atoms of an element relative to one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom
options.C: The number of protons in an atom
options.D: The total mass of all isotopes of an element

questions.explanation: Relative atomic mass (Ar) is the weighted mean mass of atoms of an element relative to one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom; it is dimensionless and reflects natural isotope abundance.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is molecular mass?

options.A: The mass of a single atom
options.B: The sum of the relative atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule
options.C: The number of atoms in a molecule

questions.explanation: Molecular mass is the sum of the relative atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule; its numerical value is commonly expressed in u.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is formula mass?

options.A: The sum of the relative atomic masses represented by a chemical formula, especially for ionic compounds
options.B: The mass of a single molecule
options.C: The number of atoms in a formula unit

questions.explanation: Formula mass is the sum of the relative atomic masses represented by a chemical formula, especially for ionic compounds that do not consist of discrete molecules.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is atomic number?

options.A: The number of neutrons in the nucleus
options.B: The number of protons in the nucleus, represented by Z
options.C: The total number of protons and neutrons
options.D: The number of electrons in the outermost shell

questions.explanation: Atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus; it is represented by Z and determines the identity of an element.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is mass number?

options.A: The number of protons in the nucleus
options.B: The total number of protons and neutrons in an atomic nucleus
options.C: The number of electrons in an atom

questions.explanation: Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in an atomic nucleus; A = Z + N.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is valency?

options.A: The number of protons in an atom
options.B: The combining capacity of an atom or radical
options.D: The number of neutrons in an atom

questions.explanation: Valency is the combining capacity of an atom or radical, often described at this level by the number of electrons lost, gained or shared in bonding; some elements show variable valency.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a chemical symbol?

options.A: A one- or two-letter abbreviation representing an element
options.B: A representation of a chemical reaction
options.C: A formula showing the composition of a compound
options.D: A number indicating the mass of an atom

questions.explanation: A chemical symbol is a one- or two-letter abbreviation representing an element; the first letter is capitalised and the second, if present, is lowercase.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Who introduced the modern system of chemical symbols?
questions.explanation: Jons Jacob Berzelius introduced the system of letter-based chemical symbols in the early nineteenth century.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a chemical formula?

options.A: A symbolic representation showing the elements present and their relative numbers in a substance
options.B: A representation of a chemical reaction
options.C: A one- or two-letter abbreviation for an element
options.D: A number indicating the mass of an atom

questions.explanation: A chemical formula is a symbolic representation showing the elements present and their relative numbers in a substance, such as H2O and NaCl.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between a formula and an equation?

options.A: A formula represents the composition of a substance; a chemical equation represents a chemical reaction
options.B: A formula represents a reaction; an equation represents a substance
options.D: A formula is used for elements only; an equation is used for compounds only

questions.explanation: A formula represents the composition of a substance; a chemical equation represents a chemical reaction using formulae for reactants and products.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the three main subatomic particles?
questions.explanation: The three main subatomic particles are protons, neutrons and electrons. Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus; electrons occupy regions around the nucleus.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the relative charge of a proton?
questions.explanation: A proton has a relative charge of +1 and a relative mass of about 1.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the relative charge of an electron?
questions.explanation: An electron has a relative charge of -1 and a relative mass of about 1/1836.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the relative charge of a neutron?
questions.explanation: A neutron has a charge of 0 and a relative mass of about 1.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Where is most of an atom's mass concentrated?

options.B: In the tiny, dense nucleus containing protons and neutrons

questions.explanation: Most of an atom's mass is concentrated in its tiny, dense nucleus, which contains protons and neutrons.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why is an ordinary atom electrically neutral?

options.A: Because it has no charged particles
options.B: Because the number of protons equals the number of electrons

questions.explanation: An ordinary atom is electrically neutral because the number of protons equals the number of electrons.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Who discovered the electron through cathode-ray experiments in 1897?
questions.explanation: J. J. Thomson discovered the electron through cathode-ray experiments in 1897.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is Thomson's atomic model commonly called?
questions.explanation: Thomson's atomic model is the 'plum pudding' model: electrons were imagined embedded in a diffuse sphere of positive charge. It could not explain Rutherford's scattering results.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What did Rutherford's gold-foil experiment establish?

options.B: That atoms are mostly empty space with a tiny, positively charged, dense nucleus
options.C: That electrons orbit in fixed energy levels
options.D: That neutrons exist in the nucleus

questions.explanation: Rutherford's gold-foil experiment showed that most alpha particles passed through thin gold foil, while a few were strongly deflected; this showed that atoms are mostly empty space with a tiny, positively charged, dense nucleus.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What limitation did Rutherford's nuclear model have?

options.A: It could not explain atomic stability and line spectra
options.B: It could not explain the existence of electrons
options.C: It could not explain the mass of the atom
options.D: It could not explain chemical bonding

questions.explanation: Rutherford's nuclear model could not explain atomic stability and line spectra.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: According to Bohr's atomic model, what happens when electrons occupy specified stationary energy levels?

options.B: They do not radiate energy while in those permitted states
options.C: They lose energy and spiral into the nucleus

questions.explanation: According to Bohr's atomic model, electrons occupy specified stationary energy levels or shells and do not radiate energy while in those permitted states; they absorb or emit energy when changing levels.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are electron shells commonly labelled as?
questions.explanation: Electron shells are allowed principal energy levels around the nucleus, commonly labelled K, L, M, N or n = 1, 2, 3, 4.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the maximum electron capacity of a shell in the Bohr model?
questions.explanation: The maximum number of electrons in a shell is 2n², where n is the shell number; capacities are K = 2, L = 8, M = 18, N = 32. Actual filling follows additional energy rules.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the maximum electron capacity of the K shell?
questions.explanation: The K shell (n=1) has a maximum capacity of 2 electrons (2n² = 2 × 1² = 2).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the maximum electron capacity of the L shell?
questions.explanation: The L shell (n=2) has a maximum capacity of 8 electrons (2n² = 2 × 2² = 8).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the maximum electron capacity of the M shell?
questions.explanation: The M shell (n=3) has a maximum capacity of 18 electrons (2n² = 2 × 3² = 18).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the maximum electron capacity of the N shell?
questions.explanation: The N shell (n=4) has a maximum capacity of 32 electrons (2n² = 2 × 4² = 32).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is electronic configuration?

options.A: The arrangement of electrons in shells or orbitals of an atom or ion
options.B: The arrangement of protons in the nucleus
options.C: The arrangement of atoms in a molecule
options.D: The arrangement of molecules in a compound

questions.explanation: Electronic configuration is the arrangement of electrons in shells or orbitals of an atom or ion; simple school-level shell configurations include sodium 2,8,1 and chlorine 2,8,7.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the electronic configuration of sodium?
questions.explanation: Sodium has the electronic configuration 2,8,1.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the electronic configuration of chlorine?
questions.explanation: Chlorine has the electronic configuration 2,8,7.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the octet rule?

options.A: Atoms tend to have eight protons in their nucleus
options.B: Atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to achieve eight electrons in their outer shell

questions.explanation: The octet rule states that many atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to achieve eight electrons in their outer shell, resembling a noble-gas configuration; there are important exceptions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are valence electrons?

options.B: Electrons in the outermost occupied shell of an atom

questions.explanation: Valence electrons are electrons in the outermost occupied shell of an atom; they play a major role in chemical bonding and reactivity.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are isotopes?

options.A: Atoms of different elements with the same mass number
options.B: Atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers due to different numbers of neutrons
options.C: Atoms with the same number of neutrons but different protons

questions.explanation: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers because they contain different numbers of neutrons; examples are carbon-12 and carbon-14.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which isotope is used in radiotherapy and sterilisation?
questions.explanation: Cobalt-60 is used in radiotherapy and sterilisation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which isotope is used in thyroid diagnosis and treatment?
questions.explanation: Iodine-131 is used in thyroid diagnosis and treatment.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which isotope is used in dating once-living materials?
questions.explanation: Carbon-14 is used in dating once-living materials.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which isotope is used as nuclear fuel?
questions.explanation: Uranium-235 is used as nuclear fuel.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are isobars?

options.A: Atoms of the same element with different mass numbers
options.B: Atoms of different elements having the same mass number but different atomic numbers
options.C: Atoms with the same number of electrons

questions.explanation: Isobars are atoms of different elements having the same mass number but different atomic numbers; for example, argon-40 and calcium-40.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an ion?

options.B: An atom or group of atoms carrying a net electric charge because electrons have been lost or gained

questions.explanation: An ion is an atom or group of atoms carrying a net electric charge because electrons have been lost or gained.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a cation?

options.A: A negatively charged ion formed by gain of electrons
options.B: A positively charged ion formed by loss of electrons

questions.explanation: A cation is a positively charged ion formed by loss of one or more electrons; examples include Na⁺, Ca²⁺ and NH₄⁺.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an anion?

options.A: A positively charged ion formed by loss of electrons
options.B: A negatively charged ion formed by gain of electrons

questions.explanation: An anion is a negatively charged ion formed by gain of one or more electrons; examples include Cl⁻, O²⁻ and SO₄²⁻.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is periodic classification?

options.A: Arrangement of elements to show recurring patterns in their properties
options.B: Arrangement of compounds by molecular mass
options.C: Arrangement of atoms in a molecule

questions.explanation: Periodic classification is the arrangement of elements to show recurring patterns in their properties, helping predict chemical and physical behaviour.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Who published an early periodic table in 1869 based on atomic mass?
questions.explanation: Dmitri Mendeleev published a periodic table in 1869, arranging elements mainly by atomic mass and chemical properties and leaving gaps for undiscovered elements.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the modern periodic law?

options.A: The properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic masses
options.B: The physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers
options.C: The properties of elements depend on the number of neutrons
options.D: The properties of elements depend on the number of electrons only

questions.explanation: The modern periodic law states that the physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Who established the importance of atomic number in periodic classification through X-ray studies?
questions.explanation: Henry Moseley established the importance of atomic number in periodic classification through X-ray studies of elements.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How many groups and periods are in the modern periodic table?
questions.explanation: There are 18 vertical groups and 7 horizontal periods in the modern periodic table.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does a group represent in the periodic table?

options.B: A vertical column where elements generally have similar valence-shell configurations

questions.explanation: A group is a vertical column. Elements in a group generally have similar valence-shell configurations and related chemical properties.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does a period represent in the periodic table?

options.B: A horizontal row where atomic number increases from left to right

questions.explanation: A period is a horizontal row. Atomic number increases from left to right across a period, and electrons are added to the same principal shell in the simple model.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Where are metals generally located in the periodic table?
questions.explanation: Metals are generally located on the left and centre of the periodic table; they are generally lustrous, malleable, ductile and good conductors, though there are exceptions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Where are non-metals generally located in the periodic table?

options.B: Mostly on the upper right side, with hydrogen on the left

questions.explanation: Non-metals are mostly on the upper right side of the periodic table, with hydrogen as a non-metal on the left; they generally have varied physical properties and tend to form covalent compounds or anions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are metalloids?

options.A: Elements with properties intermediate between metals and non-metals

questions.explanation: Metalloids are elements with properties intermediate between metals and non-metals; commonly listed examples include boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony and tellurium.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the general trend in atomic size across a period from left to right?

options.D: Atomic radius first increases then decreases

questions.explanation: Atomic radius generally decreases from left to right across a period because effective nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same main shell.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the general trend in atomic size down a group?

options.D: Atomic radius first decreases then increases

questions.explanation: Atomic radius generally increases down a group because additional electron shells are added.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does metallic character change across a period and down a group?

options.A: It increases across a period and decreases down a group
options.B: It decreases across a period and increases down a group
options.C: It increases both across a period and down a group
options.D: It decreases both across a period and down a group

questions.explanation: Metallic character generally decreases from left to right across a period and increases down a group.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does non-metallic character change across a period and down a group?

options.A: It increases across a period and decreases down a group
options.B: It decreases across a period and increases down a group
options.C: It increases both across a period and down a group
options.D: It decreases both across a period and down a group

questions.explanation: Non-metallic character generally increases from left to right across a period and decreases down a group, with exceptions and dependence on the property considered.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the general trend in valency across a main-group period?
questions.explanation: For many representative elements, valency relative to a stable octet commonly changes 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0; transition elements often show variable valency.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are noble gases?

options.B: Group 18 elements with very low chemical reactivity because their outer electron shells are filled

questions.explanation: Noble gases are Group 18 elements with very low chemical reactivity because their outer electron shells are filled; examples include helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why are noble gases generally unreactive?

options.B: They have stable outer-shell electron configurations with little tendency to gain, lose or share electrons
options.C: They have very large atomic radii

questions.explanation: Noble gases are generally unreactive because they have stable outer-shell electron configurations and therefore have little tendency to gain, lose or share electrons.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical symbol of hydrogen?
questions.explanation: The symbol of hydrogen is H.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical symbol of helium?
questions.explanation: The symbol of helium is He.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a chemical bond?

options.A: An attractive interaction that holds atoms or ions together in a substance

questions.explanation: A chemical bond is an attractive interaction that holds atoms or ions together in a substance, arising from electrostatic interactions involving nuclei and electrons.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why do atoms form chemical bonds?

options.B: Bond formation generally lowers the total energy of the system and produces a more stable arrangement

questions.explanation: Atoms form chemical bonds because bond formation generally lowers the total energy of the system and produces a more stable arrangement.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an ionic bond?

options.A: A bond formed by sharing electrons
options.B: An electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, usually formed after electron transfer
options.C: A bond between metal atoms only
options.D: A bond formed by overlapping orbitals

questions.explanation: An ionic bond is an electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, usually formed after electron transfer from one atom to another; example: NaCl.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How is sodium chloride formed?

options.A: By sharing electrons between sodium and chlorine
options.B: By sodium losing one electron to form Na⁺ and chlorine gaining one electron to form Cl⁻, followed by electrostatic attraction
options.C: By mixing sodium and chlorine without reaction

questions.explanation: Sodium loses one electron to form Na⁺ and chlorine gains one electron to form Cl⁻; electrostatic attraction between the ions forms an ionic lattice.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a covalent bond?

options.A: A bond formed by transfer of electrons
options.B: A bond formed when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons

questions.explanation: A covalent bond is a bond formed when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons; examples include H₂, O₂, CH₄ and H₂O.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a single covalent bond?

options.A: A bond formed by sharing one pair of electrons
options.B: A bond formed by sharing two pairs of electrons
options.C: A bond formed by sharing three pairs of electrons
options.D: A bond formed by transfer of electrons

questions.explanation: A single covalent bond is a covalent bond formed by sharing one pair of electrons, such as the H–H bond in H₂.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a double covalent bond?

options.A: A bond formed by sharing one pair of electrons
options.B: A bond formed by sharing two pairs of electrons
options.C: A bond formed by sharing three pairs of electrons
options.D: A bond formed by transfer of electrons

questions.explanation: A double covalent bond is a bond formed by sharing two pairs of electrons, such as the O=O bond in O₂.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a triple covalent bond?

options.A: A bond formed by sharing one pair of electrons
options.B: A bond formed by sharing two pairs of electrons
options.C: A bond formed by sharing three pairs of electrons
options.D: A bond formed by transfer of electrons

questions.explanation: A triple covalent bond is a bond formed by sharing three pairs of electrons, such as the N≡N bond in nitrogen gas.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a metallic bond?

options.A: A bond between a metal and a non-metal
options.B: The attraction between positive metal ion cores and delocalised valence electrons throughout a metallic solid
options.C: A bond formed by sharing electrons between two metals
options.D: An ionic bond between metal ions

questions.explanation: A metallic bond is the attraction between positive metal ion cores and delocalised valence electrons throughout a metallic solid; it helps explain conductivity, malleability and ductility.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are valence electrons in the context of chemical bonding?

options.A: Inner-shell electrons not involved in bonding

questions.explanation: Valence electrons are the outer-shell electrons involved in bonding; their number is a useful guide to bonding behaviour for main-group elements.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How is the formula of an ionic compound determined?

options.A: By the total positive and negative charges balancing to give an electrically neutral formula unit
options.B: By the number of protons in the metal
options.C: By the atomic mass of the elements
options.D: By the number of electrons in the outermost shell only

questions.explanation: The formula of an ionic compound is determined by the total positive and negative charges balancing to give an electrically neutral formula unit; for example, Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ form MgCl₂.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main properties of ionic compounds?

options.A: Low melting points and good conductors in solid state
options.B: Crystalline solids with high melting and boiling points; conduct electricity when molten or dissolved

questions.explanation: Ionic compounds are usually crystalline solids with high melting and boiling points; they conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water if mobile ions are present, but generally not as solids.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main properties of simple molecular covalent compounds?

options.A: High melting points and good electrical conductivity
options.B: Relatively low melting and boiling points and poor electrical conductors
options.D: Always conduct electricity when dissolved in water

questions.explanation: Simple molecular covalent compounds often have relatively low melting and boiling points and are poor electrical conductors; exceptions include giant covalent structures such as diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved but not when solid?

options.A: Because ions are fixed in position in the solid lattice but become mobile in the molten or aqueous state
options.B: Because electrons are free to move in the solid state
options.C: Because the compound decomposes on melting

questions.explanation: Ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved because ions are fixed in position in the solid lattice but become mobile in the molten or aqueous state.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a covalent compound?
questions.explanation: Water (H₂O) is a covalent compound. Examples of covalent compounds include water (H₂O), carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), ammonia (NH₃) and hydrogen chloride (HCl).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a chemical reaction?

options.A: A process in which reactants are transformed into products through rearrangement of atoms and chemical bonds

questions.explanation: A chemical reaction is a process in which reactants are transformed into products through rearrangement of atoms and chemical bonds.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a chemical equation?

options.A: A symbolic representation of a chemical reaction showing reactants, products and their relative amounts

questions.explanation: A chemical equation is a symbolic representation of a chemical reaction showing reactants, products and their relative amounts.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are reactants in a chemical reaction?

options.A: The substances formed in a reaction
options.B: The starting substances consumed or changed in a reaction
options.C: The catalyst used in a reaction

questions.explanation: Reactants are the starting substances consumed or changed in a reaction; products are the substances formed.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why must a chemical equation be balanced?

options.A: Because atoms are conserved in an ordinary chemical reaction
options.C: Because the mass of products is always greater
options.D: Because reactants always have more atoms

questions.explanation: A chemical equation must be balanced because atoms are conserved in an ordinary chemical reaction; the number of atoms of each element must be equal on both sides.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the law of conservation of mass?

options.A: In a closed system, mass is neither created nor destroyed during a chemical reaction
options.B: Mass is always lost in a chemical reaction
options.C: Mass is always gained in a chemical reaction

questions.explanation: The law of conservation of mass states that in a closed system, mass is neither created nor destroyed during a chemical reaction; total mass of reactants equals total mass of products.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How is a chemical equation balanced?

options.B: By changing coefficients in front of formulae until each element has the same number of atoms on both sides

questions.explanation: A chemical equation is balanced by changing coefficients in front of formulae until each element has the same number of atoms on both sides; subscripts in formulae must not be changed.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a combination reaction?

options.A: A reaction in which one compound breaks into simpler substances
options.B: A reaction in which two or more reactants form a single product
options.C: A reaction in which ions exchange partners
options.D: A reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element

questions.explanation: A combination reaction is a reaction in which two or more reactants form a single product; example: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a decomposition reaction?

options.A: A reaction in which two or more reactants form a single product
options.B: A reaction in which one compound breaks into two or more simpler substances
options.C: A reaction in which ions exchange partners
options.D: A reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element

questions.explanation: A decomposition reaction is a reaction in which one compound breaks into two or more simpler substances; example: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ on heating.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is thermal decomposition?
questions.explanation: Thermal decomposition is decomposition caused by heat; example: 2Pb(NO₃)₂ → 2PbO + 4NO₂ + O₂.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is electrolytic decomposition?

options.B: Decomposition caused by passing electric current through a substance

questions.explanation: Electrolytic decomposition is decomposition caused by passing electric current through a substance; example: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ during electrolysis under suitable conditions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is photochemical decomposition?
questions.explanation: Photochemical decomposition is decomposition caused by light; example: 2AgCl → 2Ag + Cl₂ in sunlight.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a displacement reaction?

options.A: A reaction in which two compounds exchange ions
options.B: A reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound
options.C: A reaction in which one compound breaks into simpler substances
options.D: A reaction in which two reactants form a single product

questions.explanation: A displacement reaction is a reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound; example: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a double displacement reaction?

options.A: A reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element
options.B: A reaction in which ions of two compounds exchange partners
options.C: A reaction in which one compound breaks into simpler substances
options.D: A reaction in which two reactants form a single product

questions.explanation: A double displacement reaction is a reaction in which ions of two compounds exchange partners; example: AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO₃.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a precipitation reaction?

options.A: A reaction that forms a gas
options.B: A reaction in aqueous solution that forms an insoluble solid called a precipitate

questions.explanation: A precipitation reaction is a reaction in aqueous solution that forms an insoluble solid called a precipitate; silver chloride is a white precipitate in the reaction of silver nitrate with sodium chloride.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a neutralisation reaction?

options.B: A reaction between an acid and a base that produces salt and water
options.D: A reaction that produces a gas only

questions.explanation: A neutralisation reaction is a reaction between an acid and a base that produces salt and water; example: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is oxidation in terms of oxygen and hydrogen?

options.A: Gain of hydrogen or loss of oxygen
options.B: Gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen

questions.explanation: At a basic level, oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen; more generally it is loss of electrons or increase in oxidation state.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is reduction in terms of oxygen and hydrogen?

options.A: Gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen
options.B: Loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen

questions.explanation: At a basic level, reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen; more generally it is gain of electrons or decrease in oxidation state.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a redox reaction?

options.A: A reaction in which only oxidation occurs
options.B: A reaction in which oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously through electron transfer or changes in oxidation states
options.C: A reaction in which only reduction occurs
options.D: A reaction that does not involve electron transfer

questions.explanation: A redox reaction is a reaction in which oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously through electron transfer or changes in oxidation states.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an oxidising agent?

options.A: A substance that causes another substance to be reduced; it donates electrons
options.B: A substance that causes another substance to be oxidised; it accepts electrons and is itself reduced
options.C: A substance that does not participate in redox reactions
options.D: A substance that is always oxidised

questions.explanation: An oxidising agent is a substance that causes another substance to be oxidised; it accepts electrons and is itself reduced.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a reducing agent?

options.A: A substance that causes another substance to be oxidised; it donates electrons and is itself oxidised
options.B: A substance that causes another substance to be reduced; it accepts electrons
options.C: A substance that does not participate in redox reactions
options.D: A substance that is always reduced

questions.explanation: A reducing agent is a substance that causes another substance to be reduced; it donates electrons and is itself oxidised.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an exothermic reaction?

options.A: A reaction that absorbs heat from its surroundings
options.B: A reaction that releases heat to its surroundings
options.C: A reaction that does not involve heat change
options.D: A reaction that only occurs in sunlight

questions.explanation: An exothermic reaction is a reaction that releases heat to its surroundings; examples include combustion and many neutralisation reactions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an endothermic reaction?

options.A: A reaction that releases heat to its surroundings
options.B: A reaction that absorbs heat from its surroundings
options.C: A reaction that does not involve heat change
options.D: A reaction that only occurs in darkness

questions.explanation: An endothermic reaction is a reaction that absorbs heat from its surroundings; examples include thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate and photosynthesis overall.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a catalyst?

options.A: A substance that is consumed in a reaction
options.B: A substance that changes the rate of a reaction by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy and is regenerated overall
options.C: A substance that changes the equilibrium position
options.D: A substance that stops a reaction completely

questions.explanation: A catalyst is a substance that changes the rate of a reaction by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy and is regenerated overall; it does not change the equilibrium position.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following factors affects the rate of a chemical reaction?

options.C: Temperature, concentration, pressure for gases, surface area, nature of reactants, catalysts and light

questions.explanation: Factors affecting the rate of a chemical reaction include temperature, concentration, pressure for gases, surface area of solids, nature of reactants, catalysts and light for photochemical reactions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why does increasing temperature often increase reaction rate?

options.B: Because a greater fraction of particles has energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, and effective collisions become more frequent

questions.explanation: Increasing temperature often increases reaction rate because a greater fraction of particles has energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, and effective collisions become more frequent.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why does powdered calcium carbonate react faster than a large lump under similar conditions?

options.A: Because powder has a larger exposed surface area, allowing more frequent effective contact with the other reactant
options.B: Because powder has a different chemical formula
options.D: Because powder has a higher temperature

questions.explanation: Powdered calcium carbonate reacts faster than a large lump because powder has a larger exposed surface area, allowing more frequent effective contact with the other reactant.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is activation energy?

options.A: The energy released in a reaction
options.B: The minimum energy that reacting particles must acquire to reach the transition state and allow a reaction to proceed

questions.explanation: Activation energy is the minimum energy that reacting particles must acquire to reach the transition state and allow a reaction to proceed.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a reversible reaction?

options.A: A reaction that proceeds only in one direction
options.B: A reaction that can proceed in both forward and reverse directions under suitable conditions
options.C: A reaction that does not reach equilibrium
options.D: A reaction that always releases heat

questions.explanation: A reversible reaction is a reaction that can proceed in both forward and reverse directions under suitable conditions; it may reach dynamic equilibrium in a closed system.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an irreversible reaction?

options.A: A reaction that proceeds in both directions
options.B: A reaction that proceeds predominantly in one direction under the stated conditions
options.C: A reaction that reaches equilibrium quickly

questions.explanation: An irreversible reaction is a reaction that proceeds predominantly in one direction under the stated conditions, often because products escape, precipitate or are strongly favoured.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is dynamic chemical equilibrium?

options.A: A state where the reaction has stopped completely
options.B: A state in a closed system where the forward and reverse reaction rates become equal, so concentrations remain constant although reactions continue at the molecular level
options.C: A state where only the forward reaction occurs
options.D: A state where only the reverse reaction occurs

questions.explanation: Dynamic chemical equilibrium is a state in a closed system where the forward and reverse reaction rates become equal, so concentrations remain constant although reactions continue at the molecular level.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an acid according to the Arrhenius concept?

options.A: A substance that increases the concentration of hydroxide ions in aqueous solution
options.B: A substance that increases the concentration of hydrogen ions (more accurately hydronium ions) in aqueous solution

questions.explanation: According to the Arrhenius concept, an acid is a substance that increases the concentration of hydrogen ions (more accurately hydronium ions) in aqueous solution.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an acid according to the Bronsted-Lowry concept?
questions.explanation: According to the Bronsted-Lowry concept, an acid is a proton (H⁺) donor.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a base according to the Arrhenius concept?

options.A: A substance that increases the concentration of hydrogen ions in aqueous solution
options.B: A substance that increases the concentration of hydroxide ions (OH⁻) in aqueous solution

questions.explanation: According to the Arrhenius concept, a base is a substance that increases the concentration of hydroxide ions (OH⁻) in aqueous solution.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a base according to the Bronsted-Lowry concept?
questions.explanation: According to the Bronsted-Lowry concept, a base is a proton (H⁺) acceptor.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an alkali?

options.A: A base that does not dissolve in water
options.B: A base that dissolves in water to produce hydroxide ions
options.C: An acid that dissolves in water
options.D: A salt that dissolves in water

questions.explanation: An alkali is a base that dissolves in water to produce hydroxide ions; examples include NaOH and KOH.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a common property of acids?

options.C: They turn blue litmus red and react with many metals to release hydrogen

questions.explanation: Common properties of acids include: aqueous acids have pH below 7 at 25°C, turn blue litmus red, react with many metals to release hydrogen and neutralise bases.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a common property of bases?

options.C: They turn red litmus blue and neutralise acids
options.D: They react with metals to release hydrogen

questions.explanation: Common properties of bases include: aqueous bases have pH above 7 at 25°C, turn red litmus blue and neutralise acids; many feel slippery, but tasting or touching chemicals is unsafe.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between a strong acid and a weak acid?

options.A: A strong acid ionises almost completely in water; a weak acid ionises only partially
options.B: A strong acid has a higher concentration than a weak acid
options.C: A strong acid has a higher pH than a weak acid
options.D: A strong acid is always more concentrated

questions.explanation: A strong acid ionises almost completely in water; a weak acid ionises only partially. Strength is not the same as concentration.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between a strong base and a weak base?

options.A: A strong base dissociates or ionises extensively in water; a weak base reacts/ionises only partially
options.B: A strong base has a lower pH than a weak base
options.C: A strong base is always more concentrated
options.D: A strong base does not dissolve in water

questions.explanation: A strong base dissociates or ionises extensively in water to provide hydroxide ions; a weak base reacts/ionises only partially.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a strong acid?
questions.explanation: Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is a strong acid. Examples of strong acids include hydrochloric acid (HCl), nitric acid (HNO₃) and sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄), whose first ionisation is strong.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a weak acid?
questions.explanation: Ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH) is a weak acid. Examples of weak acids include ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH), carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) and citric acid.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a strong base?
questions.explanation: NaOH is a strong base. Examples of strong bases include sodium hydroxide (NaOH), potassium hydroxide (KOH) and barium hydroxide [Ba(OH)₂].

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an indicator?

options.A: A substance that changes colour over a particular pH range
options.C: A substance that produces hydrogen gas
options.D: A substance that dissolves in water

questions.explanation: An indicator is a substance that changes colour over a particular pH range and is used to estimate whether a solution is acidic, neutral or alkaline.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What happens to blue litmus in an acid?
questions.explanation: Acid turns blue litmus red; alkali turns red litmus blue. Neutral solutions do not change either litmus colour.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What happens to red litmus in a base?
questions.explanation: Alkali turns red litmus blue; acid turns blue litmus red. Neutral solutions do not change either litmus colour.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the colour change of phenolphthalein in acidic and alkaline solutions?

options.A: Colourless in acidic and approximately neutral solutions; pink to magenta in alkaline solution
options.B: Red in acidic solution; yellow in alkaline solution
options.C: Yellow in acidic solution; red in alkaline solution
options.D: Blue in acidic solution; red in alkaline solution

questions.explanation: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acidic and approximately neutral solutions; pink to magenta in alkaline solution over its transition range.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the colour change of methyl orange in acidic and alkaline solutions?

options.A: Colourless in acidic solution; pink in alkaline solution
options.B: Red in acidic solution, orange near its transition range and yellow in alkaline solution
options.C: Yellow in acidic solution; red in alkaline solution
options.D: Blue in acidic solution; red in alkaline solution

questions.explanation: Methyl orange is red in acidic solution, orange near its transition range and yellow in alkaline solution.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a natural acid-base indicator?
questions.explanation: Natural acid-base indicators are obtained from natural sources; examples include litmus from lichens, turmeric and red cabbage extract.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does turmeric behave as an indicator?

options.A: It remains yellow in acidic and neutral conditions and turns reddish-brown in alkaline conditions
options.B: It turns red in acidic conditions and blue in alkaline conditions
options.C: It is colourless in acidic conditions and pink in alkaline conditions
options.D: It turns blue in acidic conditions and red in alkaline conditions

questions.explanation: Turmeric remains yellow in acidic and neutral conditions and turns reddish-brown in alkaline conditions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the pH scale?

options.A: A linear measure of hydrogen-ion activity
options.B: A logarithmic measure related to hydrogen-ion activity; at 25°C pH 7 is neutral, below 7 acidic and above 7 alkaline
options.C: A measure of hydroxide-ion concentration only

questions.explanation: The pH scale is a logarithmic measure related to hydrogen-ion activity; in dilute aqueous solutions pH is approximately -log[H⁺]. At 25°C pH 7 is neutral, below 7 acidic and above 7 alkaline.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does a change of one pH unit mean?

options.A: A twofold change in hydrogen-ion activity
options.B: A tenfold change in hydrogen-ion activity
options.C: A hundredfold change in hydrogen-ion activity

questions.explanation: A change of one pH unit means a tenfold change in hydrogen-ion activity; for example, pH 3 is about ten times more acidic than pH 4 in terms of hydrogen-ion activity.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Is pH 7 always neutral at every temperature?

options.B: No, neutral pH depends on temperature because water's ionisation changes; pH 7 is neutral at about 25°C
options.C: Yes, but only for pure water

questions.explanation: No, neutral pH depends on temperature because water's ionisation changes; pH 7 is neutral at about 25°C.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is neutralisation?

options.A: Reaction of an acid with another acid
options.B: Reaction of an acid with a base to form salt and water
options.C: Reaction of a base with another base
options.D: Reaction of a salt with water

questions.explanation: Neutralisation is the reaction of an acid with a base; for a typical strong acid-strong base reaction, H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, with salt formation from the remaining ions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a salt in chemistry?

options.A: An ionic compound formed when the replaceable hydrogen ion(s) of an acid are partly or completely replaced by metal or ammonium ions
options.B: A covalent compound formed from an acid
options.C: A base that dissolves in water

questions.explanation: A salt is an ionic compound formed when the replaceable hydrogen ion(s) of an acid are partly or completely replaced by metal or ammonium ions; salts may be acidic, basic or neutral in solution.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is common salt?
questions.explanation: Common salt is sodium chloride (NaCl), used in food seasoning, preservation and as a raw material for several chemicals.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is baking soda?

options.B: Sodium hydrogen carbonate or sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃)

questions.explanation: Baking soda is sodium hydrogen carbonate or sodium bicarbonate, NaHCO₃; used in baking, as a mild antacid and in some fire extinguishers.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What happens when baking soda is heated?

options.A: It melts to form sodium metal
options.C: It decomposes to NaCl and O₂
options.D: It reacts with oxygen to form sodium oxide

questions.explanation: When baking soda is heated: 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is washing soda?
questions.explanation: Washing soda is sodium carbonate decahydrate, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O, used in washing, water softening and manufacture of glass and chemicals.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is bleaching powder commonly represented as?

options.A: Calcium oxychloride (CaOCl₂), though commercial material is a mixture

questions.explanation: Bleaching powder is commonly represented as calcium oxychloride, CaOCl₂, though commercial material is a mixture; used for bleaching and disinfection.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How is bleaching powder prepared in the school-level description?

options.A: By passing chlorine over dry slaked lime, Ca(OH)₂, under controlled conditions
options.C: By mixing sodium chloride and water

questions.explanation: Bleaching powder is prepared by passing chlorine over dry slaked lime, Ca(OH)₂, under controlled conditions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is Plaster of Paris?
questions.explanation: Plaster of Paris is calcium sulphate hemihydrate, CaSO₄·½H₂O; it sets with water to form gypsum and is used for casts, moulds and decorative work.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is gypsum?
questions.explanation: Gypsum is calcium sulphate dihydrate, CaSO₄·2H₂O; heating it partially produces Plaster of Paris.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does Plaster of Paris set?

options.A: It reacts with water and re-forms interlocking gypsum crystals: CaSO₄·½H₂O + 1½H₂O → CaSO₄·2H₂O

questions.explanation: Plaster of Paris sets by reacting with water and re-forming interlocking gypsum crystals: CaSO₄·½H₂O + 1½H₂O → CaSO₄·2H₂O.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a common use of neutralisation in daily life?

options.A: Antacids neutralise excess stomach acid; lime is added to acidic soil

questions.explanation: Common uses of neutralisation in daily life include antacids neutralising excess stomach acid; lime is added to acidic soil; suitable bases can neutralise acidic industrial waste under controlled treatment.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why should acid be added to water rather than water to concentrated acid?

options.A: Because acid is lighter than water
options.B: Because dilution releases heat; adding acid slowly to a larger volume of water allows heat to disperse and reduces dangerous splashing

questions.explanation: Acid should be added to water rather than water to concentrated acid because dilution releases heat; adding acid slowly to a larger volume of water allows heat to disperse and reduces dangerous splashing. Always follow laboratory safety procedures.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a common physical property of metals?

options.B: Lustrous, malleable, ductile and good conductors of heat and electricity

questions.explanation: Most metals are lustrous, malleable, ductile, sonorous and good conductors of heat and electricity; mercury is liquid at room temperature and some metals are brittle.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is malleability?

options.A: The ability to be drawn into wires
options.B: The ability to be hammered or rolled into thin sheets
options.D: The ability to dissolve in water

questions.explanation: Malleability is the ability of a material, especially a metal, to be hammered or rolled into thin sheets.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is ductility?

options.A: The ability to be hammered into sheets
options.B: The ability to be drawn into wires
options.D: The ability to dissolve in acids

questions.explanation: Ductility is the ability of a material to be drawn into wires.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a common physical property of non-metals?

options.B: Many are dull, brittle when solid and poor conductors

questions.explanation: Many non-metals are dull, brittle when solid and poor conductors; important exceptions include graphite, which conducts electricity, and bromine, which is liquid at room temperature.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How do metals generally react with oxygen?

options.A: They do not react with oxygen
options.B: Many form metal oxides; for example, 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO

questions.explanation: Many metals form metal oxides when reacting with oxygen; for example, 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Some metals react slowly or form protective oxide layers.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How do non-metals generally react with oxygen?

options.B: They commonly form acidic or neutral oxides; for example, C + O₂ → CO₂ and S + O₂ → SO₂
options.C: They do not react with oxygen

questions.explanation: Non-metals commonly form acidic or neutral oxides when reacting with oxygen; for example, C + O₂ → CO₂ and S + O₂ → SO₂.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How do sodium and potassium react with cold water?

options.B: They react violently with cold water

questions.explanation: Reactivity varies: sodium and potassium react violently with cold water; calcium reacts less vigorously; magnesium reacts with hot water/steam; iron reacts with steam; copper, silver and gold do not react with water under ordinary conditions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What products are formed when a reactive metal reacts with cold water?

options.B: Metal hydroxide and hydrogen; for example, 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂

questions.explanation: When a reactive metal reacts with cold water, usually a metal hydroxide and hydrogen are formed; for example, 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How do metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with dilute acids?

options.B: They generally displace hydrogen from dilute non-oxidising acids, forming a salt and hydrogen

questions.explanation: Metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series generally displace hydrogen from dilute non-oxidising acids, forming a salt and hydrogen; copper does not liberate hydrogen from dilute HCl.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the commonly taught reactivity series of metals from more to less reactive?

options.A: K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, (H), Cu, Hg, Ag, Au
options.B: Au, Ag, Hg, Cu, (H), Pb, Fe, Zn, Al, Mg, Ca, Na, K
options.C: Na, K, Mg, Ca, Al, Fe, Zn, Pb, (H), Cu, Hg, Ag, Au
options.D: K, Na, Mg, Ca, Zn, Al, Fe, Pb, (H), Cu, Hg, Ag, Au

questions.explanation: A commonly taught order from more to less reactive is K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, (H), Cu, Hg, Ag, Au. The exact list may include additional elements.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why is hydrogen included in the reactivity series?

options.B: Because it is a reference point used to predict whether a metal can displace hydrogen from dilute acids
options.C: Because hydrogen reacts with all metals
options.D: Because hydrogen is the most reactive element

questions.explanation: Hydrogen is not a metal in the series; it is a reference point used to predict whether a metal can displace hydrogen from dilute acids.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a displacement reaction involving metals?

options.A: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution; for example, Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu
options.B: Two metals combine to form an alloy
options.C: A metal reacts with a non-metal

questions.explanation: A displacement reaction involving metals occurs when a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution; for example, Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an ore?

options.A: A naturally occurring mineral or mineral aggregate from which a metal or valuable material can be extracted economically

questions.explanation: An ore is a naturally occurring mineral or mineral aggregate from which a metal or valuable material can be extracted economically.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a mineral?

options.A: A naturally occurring substance with a characteristic chemical composition and structure

questions.explanation: A mineral is a naturally occurring substance with a characteristic chemical composition and structure; not every mineral is an economically useful ore.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is metallurgy?

options.A: The science and technology of extracting metals from ores and refining them for use

questions.explanation: Metallurgy is the science and technology of extracting metals from ores and refining them for use.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the basic steps in metal extraction?

options.A: Ore concentration, conversion to a suitable oxide or other compound, reduction to metal and refining

questions.explanation: Common stages in metal extraction include ore concentration, conversion to a suitable oxide or other compound, reduction to metal and refining; the exact process depends on the metal and ore.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How are highly reactive metals such as sodium extracted?

options.B: By electrolysis of suitable molten salts

questions.explanation: Highly reactive metals such as sodium are extracted by electrolysis of suitable molten salts, because chemical reduction with carbon is generally unsuitable.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How are moderately reactive metals such as iron commonly extracted?

options.B: Their oxides can be reduced using carbon or carbon monoxide in a furnace

questions.explanation: Moderately reactive metals such as iron are commonly extracted by reducing their oxides using carbon or carbon monoxide in a furnace; iron is produced in a blast furnace from iron ore.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How are low-reactivity metals such as gold often found?

options.B: They may occur in native or nearly uncombined form, though ores and compounds also exist

questions.explanation: Low-reactivity metals such as gold may occur in native or nearly uncombined form, though ores and compounds also exist.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an alloy?

options.B: A metallic material made by combining a metal with one or more other elements to improve properties

questions.explanation: An alloy is a metallic material made by combining a metal with one or more other elements to improve properties such as strength, hardness or corrosion resistance.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is brass?

options.A: An alloy mainly of copper and tin
options.B: An alloy mainly of copper and zinc
options.C: An alloy mainly of iron and carbon
options.D: An alloy mainly of tin and lead

questions.explanation: Brass is an alloy mainly of copper and zinc.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is bronze?

options.A: An alloy mainly of copper and zinc
options.B: An alloy mainly of copper and tin
options.C: An alloy mainly of iron and carbon
options.D: An alloy mainly of tin and lead

questions.explanation: Bronze is a traditional alloy mainly of copper and tin.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is steel?

options.A: An alloy primarily of copper and zinc
options.B: An alloy primarily of iron and carbon
options.C: An alloy primarily of copper and tin
options.D: An alloy primarily of tin and lead

questions.explanation: Steel is an alloy primarily of iron and carbon; other elements may be added to alter its properties.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is stainless steel?

options.A: A corrosion-resistant steel containing sufficient chromium (typically at least about 10.5% by mass)
options.B: A steel containing only iron and carbon
options.C: An alloy of copper and zinc
options.D: An alloy of tin and lead
