questions.explanation: Stainless steel is a corrosion-resistant steel containing sufficient chromium (typically at least about 10.5% by mass) to form a protective chromium-rich oxide film; many grades also contain nickel and other elements.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is solder?

options.A: A low-melting joining alloy used to join metal parts
options.B: An alloy of copper and zinc
options.C: An alloy of iron and carbon
options.D: An alloy of copper and tin

questions.explanation: Solder is a low-melting joining alloy used to join metal parts; traditional soft solder often contained tin and lead, while modern lead-free solders commonly use tin with silver, copper or other metals.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is corrosion?

options.A: Gradual deterioration of a material, usually a metal, due to chemical or electrochemical reaction with its environment
options.C: The extraction of a metal from its ore

questions.explanation: Corrosion is the gradual deterioration of a material, usually a metal, due to chemical or electrochemical reaction with its environment.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is rusting?

options.A: Corrosion of copper in the presence of oxygen
options.B: Corrosion of iron in the presence of oxygen and moisture, producing hydrated iron(III) oxides commonly represented as Fe₂O₃·xH₂O

questions.explanation: Rusting is the corrosion of iron in the presence of oxygen and moisture, producing hydrated iron(III) oxides commonly represented as Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What conditions promote rusting of iron?

options.C: Both oxygen and water are generally required; salts and acidic conditions can accelerate corrosion

questions.explanation: Both oxygen and water are generally required for rusting; salts and acidic conditions can accelerate corrosion.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How can rusting be prevented?

options.A: By painting, oiling/greasing, plastic coating, galvanising, electroplating, alloying or using cathodic protection

questions.explanation: Rusting can be prevented by painting, oiling/greasing, plastic coating, galvanising, electroplating, alloying or using cathodic protection.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is galvanisation?

options.A: Coating iron or steel with zinc to protect it from corrosion

questions.explanation: Galvanisation is coating iron or steel with zinc to protect it from corrosion; zinc provides a barrier and can also act sacrificially if the coating is damaged.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is electroplating?

options.A: Depositing a thin layer of one metal on another by electrolysis
options.B: Coating iron with zinc by dipping
options.C: Mixing two metals to form an alloy
options.D: Heating a metal to high temperature

questions.explanation: Electroplating is depositing a thin layer of one metal on another by electrolysis; it can improve appearance, corrosion resistance or surface properties.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the basic arrangement in electroplating?

options.A: The object to be plated is usually the cathode; the plating metal may be the anode, and an electrolyte containing ions of the plating metal is used
options.B: The object to be plated is the anode; the plating metal is the cathode
options.D: The object is heated to melt the plating metal

questions.explanation: In electroplating, the object to be plated is usually the cathode; the plating metal may be the anode, and an electrolyte containing ions of the plating metal is used.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why is carbon important in chemistry?

options.A: Because it is the most abundant element
options.B: Because it forms an exceptionally large number of compounds due to its tetravalency and ability to form strong covalent bonds with itself and many other elements
options.C: Because it is the heaviest element
options.D: Because it is the only element that forms compounds

questions.explanation: Carbon forms an exceptionally large number of compounds because it is tetravalent and forms strong covalent bonds with itself and many other elements.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the valency of carbon in most common organic compounds?
questions.explanation: Carbon is tetravalent and commonly forms four covalent bonds in most common organic compounds.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is catenation?

options.A: The ability of an element to form bonds with atoms of itself, producing chains, branches and rings
options.D: The ability to dissolve in water

questions.explanation: Catenation is the ability of an element to form bonds with atoms of itself, producing chains, branches and rings; carbon shows especially strong catenation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an allotrope?

options.A: One of two or more different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state

questions.explanation: An allotrope is one of two or more different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state; carbon has several allotropes.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is diamond?

options.A: A crystalline allotrope of carbon in which each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others in a rigid three-dimensional network
options.B: A soft, black allotrope of carbon
options.D: A compound of carbon and hydrogen

questions.explanation: Diamond is a crystalline allotrope of carbon in which each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others in a rigid three-dimensional network; it is extremely hard and does not conduct electricity well.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is graphite?

options.A: A carbon allotrope made of layers of hexagonally arranged carbon atoms; each carbon bonds to three others, with delocalised electrons allowing electrical conductivity
options.B: A hard, transparent allotrope of carbon
options.D: A compound of carbon and oxygen

questions.explanation: Graphite is a carbon allotrope made of layers of hexagonally arranged carbon atoms; each carbon bonds to three others, with delocalised electrons allowing electrical conductivity. Layers slide easily, making graphite soft.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are fullerenes?

options.A: Molecular allotropes of carbon made of hollow cage-like structures; C₆₀ is a well-known spherical fullerene

questions.explanation: Fullerenes are molecular allotropes of carbon made of hollow cage-like structures; C₆₀ is a well-known spherical fullerene.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is graphene?

options.A: A single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice with high electrical and thermal conductivity
options.B: A three-dimensional network of carbon atoms
options.C: A hollow cage of carbon atoms
options.D: A compound of carbon and oxygen

questions.explanation: Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice; it has high electrical and thermal conductivity and high mechanical strength.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an organic compound?

options.A: A carbon-based compound, commonly containing carbon-hydrogen bonds

questions.explanation: An organic compound is a carbon-based compound, commonly containing carbon-hydrogen bonds; some carbon compounds such as carbonates, carbon oxides and carbides are conventionally treated as inorganic.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a hydrocarbon?

options.A: A compound containing only carbon and hydrogen
options.B: A compound containing carbon and oxygen
options.C: A compound containing carbon and nitrogen

questions.explanation: A hydrocarbon is a compound containing only carbon and hydrogen.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a saturated hydrocarbon?

options.A: A hydrocarbon containing carbon-carbon double bonds
options.B: A hydrocarbon containing only carbon-carbon single bonds
options.C: A hydrocarbon containing carbon-carbon triple bonds

questions.explanation: A saturated hydrocarbon is a hydrocarbon containing only carbon-carbon single bonds; alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an unsaturated hydrocarbon?

options.A: A hydrocarbon containing only carbon-carbon single bonds
options.B: A hydrocarbon containing at least one carbon-carbon double or triple bond

questions.explanation: An unsaturated hydrocarbon is a hydrocarbon containing at least one carbon-carbon double or triple bond; alkenes and alkynes are examples.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are alkanes?

options.A: A homologous series of saturated open-chain hydrocarbons with general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
options.B: A homologous series of hydrocarbons containing double bonds
options.C: A homologous series of hydrocarbons containing triple bonds

questions.explanation: Alkanes are a homologous series of saturated open-chain hydrocarbons with general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; examples are methane, ethane and propane.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are alkenes?

options.A: A homologous series of open-chain hydrocarbons containing one carbon-carbon double bond, with general formula CₙH₂ₙ
options.B: A homologous series of saturated hydrocarbons
options.C: A homologous series of hydrocarbons containing triple bonds

questions.explanation: Alkenes are a homologous series of open-chain hydrocarbons containing one carbon-carbon double bond, with general formula CₙH₂ₙ for one double bond; examples are ethene and propene.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are alkynes?

options.A: A homologous series of open-chain hydrocarbons containing one carbon-carbon triple bond, with general formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂
options.B: A homologous series of saturated hydrocarbons
options.C: A homologous series of hydrocarbons containing double bonds

questions.explanation: Alkynes are a homologous series of open-chain hydrocarbons containing one carbon-carbon triple bond, with general formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ for one triple bond; ethyne is the simplest member.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a homologous series?

options.A: A family of organic compounds with the same functional group and general formula, in which successive members differ by a -CH₂ unit
options.C: A group of elements with similar properties

questions.explanation: A homologous series is a family of organic compounds with the same functional group and general formula, in which successive members differ by a -CH₂ unit and show related chemical properties.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a functional group?

options.A: An atom or group of atoms responsible for characteristic reactions of an organic compound
options.B: A group of carbon atoms only
options.C: A group of hydrogen atoms only

questions.explanation: A functional group is an atom or group of atoms responsible for characteristic reactions of an organic compound; examples include -OH, -CHO, >C=O and -COOH.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an alcohol?

options.A: An organic compound containing a hydroxyl group (-OH) bonded to a saturated carbon atom
options.B: An organic compound containing a carboxyl group
options.C: An organic compound containing an aldehyde group
options.D: An organic compound containing a ketone group

questions.explanation: An alcohol is an organic compound containing a hydroxyl group (-OH) bonded to a saturated carbon atom; ethanol is a common example.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an aldehyde?

options.A: An organic compound containing a terminal -CHO functional group
options.B: An organic compound containing a -OH group
options.C: An organic compound containing a -COOH group
options.D: An organic compound containing a >C=O group bonded to two carbon groups

questions.explanation: An aldehyde is an organic compound containing a terminal -CHO functional group; methanal and ethanal are examples.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a ketone?

options.A: An organic compound containing a carbonyl group (>C=O) bonded to two carbon groups
options.B: An organic compound containing a -CHO group
options.C: An organic compound containing a -OH group
options.D: An organic compound containing a -COOH group

questions.explanation: A ketone is an organic compound containing a carbonyl group (>C=O) bonded to two carbon groups; propanone (acetone) is a common example.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a carboxylic acid?

options.A: An organic compound containing the -COOH functional group
options.B: An organic compound containing the -OH group
options.C: An organic compound containing the -CHO group
options.D: An organic compound containing the >C=O group

questions.explanation: A carboxylic acid is an organic compound containing the -COOH functional group; ethanoic acid is a common example.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is ethanol?

options.A: An alcohol with formula C₂H₅OH; used as a solvent, fuel component and in sanitising products
options.B: A carboxylic acid with formula CH₃COOH

questions.explanation: Ethanol is an alcohol with formula C₂H₅OH; it is used as a solvent, fuel component and in sanitising products at appropriate concentrations. It is flammable and ingestion carries health risks.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is ethanoic acid?

options.A: A carboxylic acid with formula CH₃COOH; dilute aqueous ethanoic acid is the main acid in vinegar

questions.explanation: Ethanoic acid is a carboxylic acid with formula CH₃COOH; dilute aqueous ethanoic acid is the main acid in vinegar.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is esterification?

options.A: A reaction between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, commonly with an acid catalyst, producing an ester and water
options.D: A reaction between an acid and a base

questions.explanation: Esterification is a reaction between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, commonly with an acid catalyst, producing an ester and water; esters often have characteristic fruity odours.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are petroleum products?

options.A: Fractions obtained from crude oil by fractional distillation, including petroleum gas, petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oils, fuel oil and bitumen
options.C: Products obtained from natural gas only

questions.explanation: Petroleum products are fractions obtained from crude oil by fractional distillation, including petroleum gas, petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oils, fuel oil and bitumen.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is natural gas mainly composed of?

options.A: Methane (CH₄), with smaller amounts of other hydrocarbons and possible impurities

questions.explanation: Natural gas is mainly composed of methane (CH₄), with smaller amounts of other hydrocarbons and possible impurities depending on the source.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is coal?

options.A: A carbon-rich fossil fuel formed from ancient plant material under heat and pressure over geological time
options.B: A liquid fuel obtained from petroleum

questions.explanation: Coal is a carbon-rich fossil fuel formed from ancient plant material under heat and pressure over geological time; its types include peat, lignite, bituminous coal and anthracite.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are fossil fuels?

options.A: Coal, petroleum and natural gas formed from ancient organic matter over geological time

questions.explanation: Fossil fuels are coal, petroleum and natural gas formed from ancient organic matter over geological time; they are non-renewable on human timescales.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is combustion?

options.A: A chemical reaction with an oxidant, commonly oxygen, that releases energy

questions.explanation: Combustion is a chemical reaction with an oxidant, commonly oxygen, that releases energy; complete combustion of hydrocarbons produces carbon dioxide and water.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the complete combustion of methane?
questions.explanation: The complete combustion of methane is CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, releasing heat.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is incomplete combustion?

options.A: Combustion with sufficient oxygen producing only CO₂ and water
options.B: Combustion with insufficient oxygen, which can produce carbon monoxide, soot and other products
options.C: Combustion that does not release heat
options.D: Combustion that only occurs in pure oxygen

questions.explanation: Incomplete combustion is combustion with insufficient oxygen, which can produce carbon monoxide, soot and other products; carbon monoxide is a poisonous gas.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the calorific value of a fuel?

options.A: The heat released by complete combustion of a unit quantity of fuel
options.B: The mass of fuel burned per second

questions.explanation: The calorific value of a fuel is the heat released by complete combustion of a unit quantity of fuel; it is commonly expressed in kJ/kg for solid and liquid fuels or kJ/m³ for gaseous fuels.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a polymer?

options.A: A large molecule made from many repeating smaller units called monomers, joined by chemical bonds

questions.explanation: A polymer is a large molecule made from many repeating smaller units called monomers, joined by chemical bonds.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a natural polymer?
questions.explanation: Cellulose is a natural polymer. Natural polymers include cellulose, starch, proteins, natural rubber and DNA.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a synthetic polymer?
questions.explanation: Nylon is a synthetic polymer. Synthetic polymers are human-made polymers produced by chemical processes; examples include nylon, polyethylene, PVC and polyester.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is plastic?

options.A: A material whose main component is a polymer and that can be moulded or shaped during manufacture

questions.explanation: Plastic is a material whose main component is a polymer and that can be moulded or shaped during manufacture; additives may modify its properties.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between thermoplastics and thermosetting plastics?

options.A: Thermoplastics soften on heating and can generally be remoulded; thermosetting plastics form cross-linked networks and do not melt and remould easily after curing
options.B: Thermoplastics cannot be remoulded; thermosetting plastics can be remoulded

questions.explanation: Thermoplastics soften on heating and can generally be remoulded; thermosetting plastics form cross-linked networks and do not melt and remould easily after curing.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a biodegradable plastic?

options.A: A plastic designed to be broken down by microorganisms under specified environmental conditions
options.B: A plastic that never breaks down
options.D: A plastic that dissolves in all liquids

questions.explanation: A biodegradable plastic is a plastic designed to be broken down by microorganisms under specified environmental conditions; the rate and completeness depend on material and disposal conditions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a non-biodegradable plastic?

options.A: A plastic that readily breaks down by biological processes
options.B: A plastic that does not readily break down by biological processes in ordinary environmental conditions and may persist for long periods
options.C: A plastic made from natural materials only
options.D: A plastic that dissolves in water

questions.explanation: A non-biodegradable plastic is a plastic that does not readily break down by biological processes in ordinary environmental conditions and may persist for long periods.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is natural rubber mainly composed of?

options.A: Cis-1,4-polyisoprene, obtained from latex of rubber-producing plants

questions.explanation: Natural rubber is a natural polymer mainly consisting of cis-1,4-polyisoprene, obtained from latex of rubber-producing plants.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is vulcanisation of rubber?

options.A: Heating rubber with sulphur or another cross-linking system to form cross-links between polymer chains, improving elasticity, strength and durability

questions.explanation: Vulcanisation of rubber is heating rubber with sulphur or another cross-linking system to form cross-links between polymer chains, improving elasticity, strength and durability.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is nylon?

options.A: A family of synthetic polyamide polymers used in textiles, ropes, engineering components and fibres
options.B: A natural polymer found in plants

questions.explanation: Nylon is a family of synthetic polyamide polymers used in textiles, ropes, engineering components and fibres.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is polyester?

options.A: A family of polymers containing ester linkages; PET is widely used in textile fibres and beverage bottles
options.B: A natural polymer found in plants

questions.explanation: Polyester is a family of polymers containing ester linkages; PET is widely used in textile fibres and beverage bottles.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is PVC?

options.A: Polyvinyl chloride, a synthetic polymer made from vinyl chloride monomers; used in pipes, cable insulation and flooring

questions.explanation: PVC is polyvinyl chloride, a synthetic polymer made from vinyl chloride monomers; used in pipes, cable insulation, flooring and other products.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is Teflon?

options.A: The trade name commonly used for polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), a chemically resistant, low-friction polymer

questions.explanation: Teflon is the trade name commonly used for polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), a chemically resistant, low-friction polymer used in non-stick coatings, seals and industrial applications.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are common uses of polyethylene?

options.A: Packaging films, bags, bottles, containers, pipes and insulation

questions.explanation: Common uses of polyethylene include packaging films, bags, bottles, containers, pipes and insulation; it is produced in different density grades.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are common uses of polypropylene?

options.A: Packaging, household goods, automotive parts, fibres, ropes and laboratory containers

questions.explanation: Common uses of polypropylene include packaging, household goods, automotive parts, fibres, ropes and laboratory containers.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are soaps?

options.A: Sodium or potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids, produced by saponification of fats or oils with alkali

questions.explanation: Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids, produced by saponification of fats or oils with alkali.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is saponification?

options.A: Hydrolysis of fats or oils with a strong alkali to produce glycerol and fatty-acid salts (soap)
options.B: Neutralisation of an acid with a base
options.C: Formation of esters from alcohols and acids

questions.explanation: Saponification is the hydrolysis of fats or oils with a strong alkali to produce glycerol and fatty-acid salts (soap).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How do soaps clean?

options.A: Soap molecules have a hydrophilic ionic head and a hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail; they form micelles that help disperse oily dirt in water
options.B: They dissolve all types of dirt completely
options.C: They react chemically with dirt to form gases
options.D: They increase the surface tension of water

questions.explanation: Soap molecules have a hydrophilic ionic head and a hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail; they form micelles that help disperse oily dirt in water.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is hard water?

options.A: Water containing low concentrations of dissolved salts
options.B: Water containing appreciable dissolved calcium and magnesium ions, which interfere with soap lathering

questions.explanation: Hard water is water containing appreciable dissolved calcium and magnesium ions, which interfere with soap lathering and may form scale.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is soft water?

options.A: Water containing high concentrations of calcium and magnesium ions
options.B: Water containing low concentrations of hardness-causing calcium and magnesium ions; soap lathers readily in it

questions.explanation: Soft water is water containing low concentrations of hardness-causing calcium and magnesium ions; soap lathers readily in it.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is temporary hardness of water?

options.A: Hardness mainly caused by dissolved calcium and magnesium hydrogencarbonates; boiling can remove much of it
options.B: Hardness caused by calcium and magnesium chlorides
options.C: Hardness that cannot be removed by any method

questions.explanation: Temporary hardness of water is hardness mainly caused by dissolved calcium and magnesium hydrogencarbonates; boiling can remove much of it by precipitating insoluble compounds.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is permanent hardness of water?

options.A: Hardness mainly due to dissolved calcium and magnesium hydrogencarbonates
options.B: Hardness mainly due to dissolved calcium and magnesium chlorides and sulphates; it is not removed by ordinary boiling

questions.explanation: Permanent hardness of water is hardness mainly due to dissolved calcium and magnesium chlorides and sulphates; it is not removed by ordinary boiling.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How can water hardness be reduced?

options.A: By boiling for temporary hardness, washing soda treatment, ion-exchange resins and reverse osmosis

questions.explanation: Water hardness can be reduced by methods including boiling for temporary hardness, washing soda treatment, ion-exchange resins and reverse osmosis.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are detergents?

options.A: Synthetic cleansing agents, commonly surfactants, that reduce surface tension and help remove grease

questions.explanation: Detergents are synthetic cleansing agents, commonly surfactants, that reduce surface tension and help remove grease; many work better than soaps in hard water.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main difference between soap and detergent in hard water?

options.A: Soap forms insoluble scum with calcium and magnesium ions; many synthetic detergents do not form such insoluble salts and remain effective
options.B: Soap works better in hard water than detergents
options.C: Detergents form scum in hard water
options.D: Both behave identically in hard water

questions.explanation: Soap forms insoluble scum with calcium and magnesium ions; many synthetic detergents do not form such insoluble salts and remain effective in hard water.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main stages in municipal drinking-water treatment?

options.A: Screening, coagulation/flocculation, sedimentation, filtration and disinfection

questions.explanation: Common stages in municipal drinking-water treatment include screening, coagulation/flocculation, sedimentation, filtration and disinfection; treatment varies with source-water quality.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is chlorination of water?

options.A: Disinfection by adding chlorine or chlorine-releasing compounds to inactivate many disease-causing microorganisms

questions.explanation: Chlorination of water is disinfection by adding chlorine or chlorine-releasing compounds to inactivate many disease-causing microorganisms; dosage and contact time must be controlled.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Does boiling water remove dissolved salts?

options.A: Yes, boiling removes all dissolved salts
options.B: No, boiling kills many pathogens but does not remove dissolved non-volatile salts; evaporation can even concentrate them
options.C: Yes, boiling removes only calcium salts

questions.explanation: Boiling water does not remove dissolved salts; boiling kills many pathogens but does not remove dissolved non-volatile salts; evaporation can even concentrate them.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is distillation in water purification?

options.A: Water is vaporised and the vapour condensed, leaving many non-volatile impurities behind
options.D: Water is boiled and then cooled

questions.explanation: In distillation, water is vaporised and the vapour condensed, leaving many non-volatile impurities behind; volatile contaminants may require additional treatment.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are fertilisers?

options.A: Substances added to soil or plants to supply essential nutrients and improve plant growth

questions.explanation: Fertilisers are substances added to soil or plants to supply essential nutrients and improve plant growth; major nutrients include nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium (NPK).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does NPK stand for on fertiliser labels?
questions.explanation: NPK stands for Nitrogen (N), phosphorus expressed as phosphate equivalent (P₂O₅) and potassium expressed as potash equivalent (K₂O), according to common fertiliser labelling conventions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is urea fertiliser and what is its approximate nitrogen content?

options.A: A nitrogen fertiliser with formula CO(NH₂)₂, containing about 46% nitrogen by mass in pure form
options.D: A mixed fertiliser containing equal NPK

questions.explanation: Urea fertiliser is a nitrogen fertiliser with formula CO(NH₂)₂, containing about 46% nitrogen by mass in pure form.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a chemical pesticide?

options.A: A substance or mixture used to prevent, destroy, repel or control pests

questions.explanation: A chemical pesticide is a substance or mixture used to prevent, destroy, repel or control pests; it includes insecticides, herbicides and fungicides.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an insecticide?

options.A: A pesticide used to control insects
options.B: A pesticide used to control weeds
options.C: A pesticide used to control fungi
options.D: A pesticide used to control bacteria

questions.explanation: An insecticide is a pesticide used to control insects.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a herbicide?

options.A: A pesticide used to control insects
options.B: A pesticide used to control unwanted plants or weeds
options.C: A pesticide used to control fungi
options.D: A pesticide used to control bacteria

questions.explanation: A herbicide is a pesticide used to control unwanted plants or weeds.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a fungicide?

options.A: A pesticide used to control insects
options.B: A pesticide used to control weeds
options.C: A pesticide used to prevent or control fungal diseases
options.D: A pesticide used to control bacteria

questions.explanation: A fungicide is a pesticide used to prevent or control fungal diseases.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a medicine?

options.A: A substance or preparation used to prevent, diagnose, treat or relieve disease or symptoms
options.B: A substance used to fertilise soil
options.C: A substance used to preserve food
options.D: A substance used to purify water

questions.explanation: A medicine is a substance or preparation used to prevent, diagnose, treat or relieve disease or symptoms; medicines should be used according to qualified medical advice and directions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are antibiotics?

options.A: Medicines that kill bacteria or inhibit their growth; they do not treat viral infections

questions.explanation: Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or inhibit their growth; they do not treat viral infections such as common colds or influenza.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are antacids?

options.A: Substances that neutralise excess stomach acid

questions.explanation: Antacids are substances that neutralise excess stomach acid; examples include magnesium hydroxide, aluminium hydroxide and calcium carbonate.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are analgesics?
questions.explanation: Analgesics are medicines that relieve pain; examples include paracetamol and ibuprofen, which have different mechanisms and precautions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are antiseptics?

options.A: Chemical agents applied to living tissue to reduce or inhibit microorganisms
options.B: Chemical agents used on inanimate surfaces only

questions.explanation: Antiseptics are chemical agents applied to living tissue to reduce or inhibit microorganisms; examples include appropriately formulated povidone-iodine and chlorhexidine products.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are disinfectants?

options.A: Chemical agents used on inanimate surfaces or objects to destroy or reduce microorganisms
options.B: Chemical agents applied to living tissue only

questions.explanation: Disinfectants are chemical agents used on inanimate surfaces or objects to destroy or reduce microorganisms; they are not automatically safe for use on skin.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between antiseptics and disinfectants?

options.A: Antiseptics are formulated for living tissue; disinfectants are intended for non-living surfaces
options.B: Antiseptics are for non-living surfaces; disinfectants are for living tissue
options.D: Disinfectants are always safe for skin

questions.explanation: Antiseptics are formulated for living tissue; disinfectants are intended for non-living surfaces. Concentration and formulation matter.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are food preservatives?

options.A: Substances added to food to slow spoilage caused by microorganisms, oxidation or other reactions
options.B: Substances that add colour to food
options.C: Substances that add flavour to food
options.D: Substances that improve texture of food

questions.explanation: Food preservatives are substances added to food to slow spoilage caused by microorganisms, oxidation or other reactions; examples include salt, sugar, sodium benzoate and sulphur dioxide in permitted uses.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are food additives?

options.A: Substances added to food for technological purposes such as preservation, colouring, flavouring, stabilising, emulsifying or improving texture
options.B: Substances that are naturally present in food
options.D: Substances that are used only for medicine

questions.explanation: Food additives are substances added to food for technological purposes such as preservation, colouring, flavouring, stabilising, emulsifying or improving texture.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are artificial sweeteners?

options.A: Sweet-tasting substances used as sugar substitutes, often with little or no energy at the quantities used
options.C: Substances that add colour to food

questions.explanation: Artificial sweeteners are sweet-tasting substances used as sugar substitutes, often with little or no energy at the quantities used; examples include saccharin, aspartame and sucralose.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is food adulteration?

options.A: Addition, substitution or removal of substances that reduces food quality or makes it unsafe or misleading

questions.explanation: Food adulteration is the addition, substitution or removal of substances that reduces food quality or makes it unsafe or misleading; examples include unauthorised colours or dilution with unsafe materials.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why are unauthorised food colours dangerous?

options.A: Some may contain toxic or carcinogenic substances or cause adverse effects; only permitted food colours should be used within regulatory limits

questions.explanation: Unauthorised food colours can be dangerous because some may contain toxic or carcinogenic substances or cause adverse effects; only permitted food colours should be used within regulatory limits.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is baking powder?

options.A: A leavening mixture generally containing sodium hydrogen carbonate, an edible acid or acid salts, and often starch
options.C: A mixture of sodium chloride and water

questions.explanation: Baking powder is a leavening mixture generally containing sodium hydrogen carbonate, an edible acid or acid salts, and often starch; it releases carbon dioxide when moistened and/or heated.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between baking soda and baking powder?

options.A: Baking soda is sodium hydrogen carbonate alone; baking powder includes baking soda plus acidifying components and usually a starch carrier
options.B: Baking soda is a mixture; baking powder is a pure compound

questions.explanation: Baking soda is sodium hydrogen carbonate alone; baking powder includes baking soda plus acidifying components and usually a starch carrier.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are common household bleaching agents?

options.A: Sodium hypochlorite solutions and oxygen-based bleaching agents such as hydrogen peroxide or percarbonate products

questions.explanation: Common household bleaching agents include sodium hypochlorite solutions and oxygen-based bleaching agents such as hydrogen peroxide or percarbonate products; never mix bleach with acids or ammonia because toxic gases may form.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical basis of cooking?

options.A: Heat-driven changes such as protein denaturation, starch gelatinisation, caramelisation, Maillard browning, fat melting and microbial destruction

questions.explanation: The chemical basis of cooking involves heat-driven changes such as protein denaturation, starch gelatinisation, caramelisation, Maillard browning, fat melting and microbial destruction.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the Maillard reaction?

options.A: A set of reactions between reducing sugars and amino compounds that produces brown colour and characteristic flavours in cooked foods
options.B: Thermal decomposition of sugars on heating

questions.explanation: The Maillard reaction is a set of reactions between reducing sugars and amino compounds that produces brown colour and characteristic flavours in cooked foods.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is caramelisation?

options.A: Thermal decomposition and transformation of sugars on heating, producing brown-coloured compounds and characteristic flavours
options.B: Reaction between sugars and amino acids

questions.explanation: Caramelisation is the thermal decomposition and transformation of sugars on heating, producing brown-coloured compounds and characteristic flavours.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate composition of dry air near sea level?

options.A: About 78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.93% argon and about 0.04% carbon dioxide by volume

questions.explanation: The approximate composition of dry air near sea level is about 78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.93% argon and about 0.04% carbon dioxide by volume; water vapour varies.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which gas is most abundant in Earth's atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is the most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere, at approximately 78% by volume in dry air.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which gas is essential for aerobic respiration and supports ordinary combustion?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is essential for aerobic respiration and supports ordinary combustion; it makes up about 21% of dry air.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate composition of pure water by mass?

options.A: About 11.1% hydrogen and 88.9% oxygen by mass
options.B: About 50% hydrogen and 50% oxygen by mass
options.C: About 88.9% hydrogen and 11.1% oxygen by mass
options.D: About 75% hydrogen and 25% oxygen by mass

questions.explanation: Pure water has the approximate composition of about 11.1% hydrogen and 88.9% oxygen by mass; the formula is H₂O.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the oxygen cycle?

options.A: The movement of oxygen among the atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and lithosphere through photosynthesis, respiration, combustion, oxidation and other processes
options.B: The movement of nitrogen in the atmosphere
options.C: The movement of carbon in the atmosphere
options.D: The movement of water in the environment

questions.explanation: The oxygen cycle is the movement of oxygen among the atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and lithosphere through photosynthesis, respiration, combustion, oxidation and other processes.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the carbon cycle?

options.A: The movement of carbon among atmosphere, oceans, organisms, soils and rocks through photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, ocean exchange, combustion and geological processes
options.B: The movement of nitrogen in the atmosphere
options.C: The movement of oxygen in the atmosphere
options.D: The movement of water in the environment

questions.explanation: The carbon cycle is the movement of carbon among atmosphere, oceans, organisms, soils and rocks through photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, ocean exchange, combustion and geological processes.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the nitrogen cycle?

options.A: The movement of nitrogen through fixation, assimilation, ammonification, nitrification and denitrification among atmosphere, soil, water and living organisms
options.B: The movement of carbon in the atmosphere
options.C: The movement of oxygen in the atmosphere
options.D: The movement of water in the environment

questions.explanation: The nitrogen cycle is the movement of nitrogen through fixation, assimilation, ammonification, nitrification and denitrification among atmosphere, soil, water and living organisms.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is nitrogen fixation?

options.A: Conversion of atmospheric nitrogen (N₂) into biologically usable nitrogen compounds, by nitrogen-fixing microbes, lightning or industrial processes
options.B: Conversion of nitrate to nitrogen gas

questions.explanation: Nitrogen fixation is the conversion of atmospheric nitrogen (N₂) into biologically usable nitrogen compounds, by nitrogen-fixing microbes, lightning or industrial processes.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is nitrification?

options.A: Microbial oxidation of ammonia/ammonium to nitrite and then nitrate, mainly by specialised microorganisms
options.B: Conversion of nitrate to nitrogen gas
options.C: Conversion of nitrogen gas to ammonia

questions.explanation: Nitrification is the microbial oxidation of ammonia/ammonium to nitrite and then nitrate, mainly by specialised microorganisms.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is denitrification?

options.A: Microbial reduction of nitrate or nitrite to gaseous nitrogen forms, returning nitrogen to the atmosphere, often under low-oxygen conditions
options.B: Conversion of nitrogen gas to ammonia

questions.explanation: Denitrification is the microbial reduction of nitrate or nitrite to gaseous nitrogen forms, returning nitrogen to the atmosphere, often under low-oxygen conditions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the water cycle?

options.A: Continuous movement of water through evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, infiltration, runoff and groundwater flow
options.B: The movement of carbon in the atmosphere
options.C: The movement of nitrogen in the atmosphere
options.D: The movement of oxygen in the atmosphere

questions.explanation: The water cycle is the continuous movement of water through evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, infiltration, runoff and groundwater flow.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are greenhouse gases?

options.A: Atmospheric gases that absorb and emit infrared radiation; major examples include water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, ozone and fluorinated gases
options.B: Gases that absorb ultraviolet radiation only
options.C: Gases that do not interact with radiation
options.D: Gases found only in the stratosphere

questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases are atmospheric gases that absorb and emit infrared radiation; major examples include water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, ozone and fluorinated gases.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the greenhouse effect?

options.A: Warming that occurs because greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared radiation emitted by Earth's surface
options.C: The absorption of ultraviolet radiation by ozone
options.D: The reflection of sunlight by clouds

questions.explanation: The greenhouse effect is warming that occurs because greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared radiation emitted by Earth's surface; the natural effect makes Earth habitable, while human emissions strengthen it.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is global warming?

options.A: The long-term increase in Earth's average surface temperature, primarily driven in recent decades by human-caused increases in greenhouse-gas concentrations
options.B: A temporary increase in temperature during summer
options.D: The depletion of the ozone layer

questions.explanation: Global warming is the long-term increase in Earth's average surface temperature, primarily driven in recent decades by human-caused increases in greenhouse-gas concentrations.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is acid rain?

options.A: Rain or other precipitation made unusually acidic mainly by sulphuric and nitric acids formed from atmospheric SO₂ and nitrogen oxides
options.D: Rain that contains only carbon dioxide

questions.explanation: Acid rain is rain or other precipitation made unusually acidic mainly by sulphuric and nitric acids formed from atmospheric SO₂ and nitrogen oxides; conventionally, rain below about pH 5.6 is termed acid rain.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are major sources of acid-rain-forming gases?

options.A: Burning fossil fuels in power plants, industries and vehicles releases sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides; natural sources also contribute

questions.explanation: Major sources of acid-rain-forming gases include burning fossil fuels in power plants, industries and vehicles, which releases sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides; natural sources also contribute.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the effects of acid rain?

options.A: It acidifies lakes and soils, harms aquatic organisms, leaches nutrients, mobilises toxic aluminium and corrodes buildings and monuments

questions.explanation: The effects of acid rain include acidifying lakes and soils, harming aquatic organisms, leaching nutrients, mobilising toxic aluminium and corroding buildings and monuments, especially limestone and marble.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the ozone layer?

options.A: A region of the stratosphere with relatively high ozone concentration that absorbs much of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet-B radiation
options.B: A layer of oxygen in the troposphere
options.C: A layer of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere
options.D: A layer of nitrogen in the stratosphere

questions.explanation: The ozone layer is a region of the stratosphere with relatively high ozone concentration that absorbs much of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet-B radiation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What causes ozone-layer depletion?

options.A: Ozone-depleting substances such as chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and halons release chlorine or bromine radicals in the stratosphere that catalytically destroy ozone

questions.explanation: Ozone-layer depletion is caused by ozone-depleting substances such as chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and halons that release chlorine or bromine radicals in the stratosphere that catalytically destroy ozone.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the Montreal Protocol?

options.A: An international treaty adopted in 1987 to phase out production and consumption of ozone-depleting substances
options.B: A treaty to reduce greenhouse gas emissions
options.D: A treaty to reduce acid rain

questions.explanation: The Montreal Protocol is an international treaty adopted in 1987 to phase out production and consumption of ozone-depleting substances; it is widely regarded as a major environmental agreement.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is photochemical smog?

options.A: Air pollution formed when sunlight drives reactions involving nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, producing ground-level ozone and other oxidants

questions.explanation: Photochemical smog is air pollution formed when sunlight drives reactions involving nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, producing ground-level ozone and other oxidants.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are major air pollutants?

options.A: Particulate matter (PM₂.₅ and PM₁₀), sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, ground-level ozone, volatile organic compounds, lead and other toxic substances

questions.explanation: Major air pollutants include particulate matter (PM₂.₅ and PM₁₀), sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, ground-level ozone, volatile organic compounds, lead and other toxic substances.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is particulate matter?

options.A: A mixture of tiny solid particles and liquid droplets suspended in air; PM₂.₅ has aerodynamic diameter up to 2.5 micrometres and PM₁₀ up to 10 micrometres

questions.explanation: Particulate matter is a mixture of tiny solid particles and liquid droplets suspended in air; PM₂.₅ has aerodynamic diameter up to 2.5 micrometres and PM₁₀ up to 10 micrometres.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous?

options.A: It binds strongly to haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity; it is colourless and odourless
options.D: It reacts with water to form acid

questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it binds strongly to haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity; it is colourless and odourless.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is water pollution?

options.A: Contamination of water bodies by physical, chemical or biological agents that makes water harmful or unsuitable for uses and ecosystems
options.B: Addition of clean water to a river

questions.explanation: Water pollution is the contamination of water bodies by physical, chemical or biological agents that makes water harmful or unsuitable for uses and ecosystems.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are common water pollutants?

options.A: Pathogens, sewage, fertilisers, pesticides, industrial chemicals, heavy metals, oil, plastics, sediments and excess nutrients

questions.explanation: Common water pollutants include pathogens, sewage, fertilisers, pesticides, industrial chemicals, heavy metals, oil, plastics, sediments and excess nutrients.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is eutrophication?

options.A: Excess nutrient enrichment, especially by nitrogen and phosphorus, causing algal blooms and oxygen depletion that can harm aquatic life
options.B: The addition of oxygen to water
options.C: The removal of nutrients from water
options.D: The formation of ice on water bodies

questions.explanation: Eutrophication is excess nutrient enrichment, especially by nitrogen and phosphorus, causing algal blooms and oxygen depletion that can harm aquatic life.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is biochemical oxygen demand (BOD)?

options.A: The amount of dissolved oxygen used by microorganisms to biologically decompose organic matter in water under specified test conditions; high BOD often indicates organic pollution
options.B: The amount of oxygen produced by plants in water
options.C: The amount of oxygen dissolved in water from the atmosphere
options.D: The amount of oxygen required for photosynthesis

questions.explanation: Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) is the amount of dissolved oxygen used by microorganisms to biologically decompose organic matter in water under specified test conditions; high BOD often indicates organic pollution.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is soil contamination?

options.A: Presence of harmful chemicals or wastes in soil at levels that can damage organisms, reduce soil quality or contaminate crops and groundwater
options.B: Presence of natural minerals in soil
options.C: Addition of organic compost to soil

questions.explanation: Soil contamination is the presence of harmful chemicals or wastes in soil at levels that can damage organisms, reduce soil quality or contaminate crops and groundwater.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are examples of soil contaminants?

options.A: Heavy metals such as lead, cadmium and mercury; pesticide residues; petroleum hydrocarbons; industrial solvents and excessive fertiliser nutrients

questions.explanation: Examples of soil contaminants include heavy metals such as lead, cadmium and mercury; pesticide residues; petroleum hydrocarbons; industrial solvents and excessive fertiliser nutrients.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is chemical waste?

options.A: Discarded chemical substances or mixtures from households, laboratories, agriculture, healthcare and industries that may be hazardous or non-hazardous

questions.explanation: Chemical waste is discarded chemical substances or mixtures from households, laboratories, agriculture, healthcare and industries that may be hazardous or non-hazardous.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are toxic substances?

options.A: Substances capable of causing harmful effects in organisms at sufficient exposure; toxicity depends on dose, route, duration and susceptibility
options.C: Substances that are found in nature only
options.D: Substances that have no chemical properties

questions.explanation: Toxic substances are substances capable of causing harmful effects in organisms at sufficient exposure; toxicity depends on dose, route, duration and susceptibility.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is bioaccumulation?

options.A: Build-up of a chemical in an organism over time when uptake exceeds elimination
options.B: Increase in concentration of a substance at higher trophic levels
options.D: Removal of chemicals from an organism

questions.explanation: Bioaccumulation is the build-up of a chemical in an organism over time when uptake exceeds elimination.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is biomagnification?

options.A: Increase in concentration of a persistent substance at successively higher trophic levels in a food chain
options.B: Build-up of a chemical in a single organism
options.D: Removal of chemicals from an ecosystem

questions.explanation: Biomagnification is the increase in concentration of a persistent substance at successively higher trophic levels in a food chain; certain persistent organic pollutants and methylmercury can biomagnify.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are biodegradable substances?

options.A: Substances that microorganisms can break down into simpler products under suitable conditions
options.B: Substances that never break down in nature

questions.explanation: Biodegradable substances are substances that microorganisms can break down into simpler products under suitable conditions; biodegradability depends on the material and environment.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are non-biodegradable substances?

options.A: Substances that microorganisms can easily break down
options.B: Substances that resist biological breakdown or persist for long periods under ordinary environmental conditions
options.D: Substances that dissolve in water easily

questions.explanation: Non-biodegradable substances are substances that resist biological breakdown or persist for long periods under ordinary environmental conditions; many plastics and certain persistent chemicals are examples.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the chemical effects of pollution?

options.A: Pollution can alter pH, oxygen balance and nutrient cycles; cause toxicity, corrosion and eutrophication; generate smog and acid deposition; and damage ecosystems and human health

questions.explanation: Chemical effects of pollution include altering pH, oxygen balance and nutrient cycles; causing toxicity, corrosion and eutrophication; generating smog and acid deposition; and damaging ecosystems and human health.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How can chemical pollution be reduced?

options.A: Use cleaner production, minimise hazardous chemicals, treat industrial effluents and sewage, apply fertilisers and pesticides responsibly, segregate and safely dispose of hazardous waste, and monitor air, water and soil quality

questions.explanation: Chemical pollution can be reduced by using cleaner production, minimising hazardous chemicals, treating industrial effluents and sewage, applying fertilisers and pesticides responsibly, segregating and safely disposing of hazardous waste, and monitoring air, water and soil quality.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is plasma?

options.A: A state of matter found in conditions such as stars and electrical discharges
options.B: A type of gas at room temperature

questions.explanation: Plasma is another state of matter found in conditions such as stars and electrical discharges, in addition to the three common states solid, liquid and gas.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the value of the Avogadro constant?
questions.explanation: The Avogadro constant is 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ (exact).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the unified atomic mass unit (u) defined as?

options.A: 1/12 the mass of a carbon-12 atom; approximately 1.6605 × 10⁻²⁷ kg
options.B: The mass of a hydrogen atom

questions.explanation: 1 u = 1/12 the mass of a carbon-12 atom; approximately 1.6605 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate value of the elementary charge?
questions.explanation: The elementary charge is approximately 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulomb.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical formula of water?
questions.explanation: Water has the formula H₂O; relative molecular mass approximately 18.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical formula of carbon dioxide?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide has the formula CO₂; relative molecular mass approximately 44.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical formula of ammonia?
questions.explanation: Ammonia has the formula NH₃; relative molecular mass approximately 17.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical formula of methane?
questions.explanation: Methane has the formula CH₄; relative molecular mass approximately 16.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical formula of common salt?
questions.explanation: Common salt is sodium chloride, NaCl.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical formula of baking soda?
questions.explanation: Baking soda is sodium hydrogen carbonate, NaHCO₃.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical formula of washing soda?
questions.explanation: Washing soda is sodium carbonate decahydrate, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical formula of gypsum?
questions.explanation: Gypsum is calcium sulphate dihydrate, CaSO₄·2H₂O.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical formula of Plaster of Paris?
questions.explanation: Plaster of Paris is calcium sulphate hemihydrate, CaSO₄·½H₂O.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main acid in vinegar?
questions.explanation: Vinegar acid is ethanoic (acetic) acid, CH₃COOH.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical formula of urea?
questions.explanation: Urea has the formula CO(NH₂)₂; it is a common nitrogen fertiliser.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is rust commonly represented as?
questions.explanation: Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, commonly represented as Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical formula of ozone?
questions.explanation: Ozone has the formula O₃; it is a triatomic form of oxygen.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical formula of hydrogen peroxide?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen peroxide has the formula H₂O₂; used in some disinfecting and bleaching formulations.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which subatomic particle has a relative mass of about 1/1836?
questions.explanation: An electron has a charge of -1 and a relative mass of about 1/1836.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a property of giant covalent structures?

options.B: High melting points and hardness (e.g., diamond)

questions.explanation: Giant covalent structures such as diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide are exceptions to the general properties of simple molecular covalent compounds; they have high melting points and other distinctive properties.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical equation for the neutralisation of HCl with NaOH?
questions.explanation: The neutralisation reaction between HCl and NaOH produces salt and water: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical equation for the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate?
questions.explanation: On heating, calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical equation for the reaction of zinc with copper sulphate?
questions.explanation: Zinc displaces copper from copper sulphate: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical equation for the reaction of silver nitrate with sodium chloride?
questions.explanation: Silver nitrate reacts with sodium chloride to form a white precipitate of silver chloride: AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO₃.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical equation for the thermal decomposition of lead nitrate?
questions.explanation: On heating, lead nitrate decomposes: 2Pb(NO₃)₂ → 2PbO + 4NO₂ + O₂.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical equation for the electrolytic decomposition of water?
questions.explanation: During electrolysis under suitable conditions: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical equation for the photochemical decomposition of silver chloride?
questions.explanation: In sunlight, silver chloride decomposes: 2AgCl → 2Ag + Cl₂.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the general neutralisation equation for a strong acid-strong base reaction?
questions.explanation: For a typical strong acid-strong base reaction, H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, with salt formation from the remaining ions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which metal is liquid at room temperature?
questions.explanation: Mercury is liquid at room temperature; most other metals are solid. Some metals are brittle.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which non-metal conducts electricity?
questions.explanation: Graphite is an important exception among non-metals; it conducts electricity due to delocalised electrons.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which non-metal is liquid at room temperature?
questions.explanation: Bromine is a non-metal that is liquid at room temperature; it is an important exception among non-metals.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why does diamond not conduct electricity well while graphite does?

options.A: Diamond has no free electrons; graphite has delocalised electrons
options.B: Diamond is a metal; graphite is a non-metal
options.C: Diamond has ions; graphite has molecules
options.D: Diamond is liquid; graphite is solid

questions.explanation: Diamond does not conduct electricity well because each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others in a rigid three-dimensional network with no free electrons. Graphite conducts electricity because each carbon bonds to three others, with delocalised electrons allowing electrical conductivity.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the general formula of alkanes?
questions.explanation: Alkanes are a homologous series of saturated open-chain hydrocarbons with general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the general formula of alkenes (with one double bond)?
questions.explanation: Alkenes are a homologous series of open-chain hydrocarbons containing one carbon-carbon double bond, with general formula CₙH₂ₙ for one double bond.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the general formula of alkynes (with one triple bond)?
questions.explanation: Alkynes are a homologous series of open-chain hydrocarbons containing one carbon-carbon triple bond, with general formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ for one triple bond.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the simplest member of the alkyne series?
questions.explanation: Ethyne (acetylene) is the simplest member of the alkyne series.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the hydrophilic part of a soap molecule?
questions.explanation: Soap molecules have a hydrophilic ionic head and a hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail; the ionic head is attracted to water, while the hydrocarbon tail is attracted to oily dirt.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the hydrophobic part of a soap molecule?
questions.explanation: Soap molecules have a hydrophilic ionic head and a hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail; the hydrocarbon tail is attracted to oily dirt.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between stratospheric ozone and ground-level ozone?

options.A: Stratospheric ozone protects from UV radiation; ground-level ozone is an air pollutant
options.B: Stratospheric ozone is a pollutant; ground-level ozone protects from UV radiation

questions.explanation: Ozone in the stratosphere protects from UV radiation; ground-level ozone is an air pollutant. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between strong/weak and concentrated/dilute in acid-base chemistry?

options.A: Strong/weak refers to extent of ionisation; concentrated/dilute refers to amount of solute per amount of solution
options.B: Strong/weak refers to concentration; concentrated/dilute refers to ionisation

questions.explanation: Strong/weak refers to extent of ionisation; concentrated/dilute refers to amount of solute per amount of solution. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What accelerates the rusting of iron?
questions.explanation: Both oxygen and water are generally required for rusting; salts and acidic conditions can accelerate corrosion.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why should household bleach never be mixed with acids or ammonia?

options.A: Because toxic gases may be released

questions.explanation: Never mix household bleach with acids or ammonia because toxic gases can be released. This is an important safety precaution.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: In a neutral atom, the number of electrons is equal to the number of:
questions.explanation: In a neutral atom, electrons equal protons. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Isotopes have the same atomic number but different:
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers; isobars have the same mass number but different atomic numbers. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: The modern periodic table is arranged by increasing:
questions.explanation: The modern periodic table is arranged by increasing atomic number, not atomic mass. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or in aqueous solution?

options.A: Because electrons are free to move

questions.explanation: Ionic compounds conduct when molten or in aqueous solution because ions can move; solid ionic crystals generally do not conduct. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: When balancing a chemical equation, what must be changed?
questions.explanation: Balancing an equation means changing coefficients, never changing subscripts in a chemical formula. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: At about 25°C, what is the pH range for acidic solutions?
questions.explanation: At about 25°C pH below 7 is acidic, pH 7 neutral and pH above 7 alkaline; pH is logarithmic. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Soap forms scum with which ions in hard water?
questions.explanation: Soap forms scum with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ in hard water; many synthetic detergents work better in hard water. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: More reactive metals can displace less reactive metals from:
questions.explanation: More reactive metals can displace less reactive metals from their salt solutions. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which allotrope of carbon is very hard and does not conduct electricity well?
questions.explanation: Diamond is very hard and does not conduct electricity well; graphite is soft and conducts electricity. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which allotrope of carbon is soft and conducts electricity?
questions.explanation: Graphite is soft and conducts electricity; diamond is very hard and does not conduct electricity well. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Antibiotics act against:
questions.explanation: Antibiotics act against bacteria, not viruses. Do not use antibiotics without appropriate medical advice. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Acid rain is associated mainly with which gases?
questions.explanation: Acid rain is associated mainly with SO₂ and nitrogen oxides; photochemical smog is associated with sunlight, NOx and VOCs. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Photochemical smog is associated with which combination?
questions.explanation: Photochemical smog is associated with sunlight, NOx and VOCs; acid rain is associated mainly with SO₂ and nitrogen oxides. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it:

options.B: Is colourless and odourless and interferes with oxygen transport by haemoglobin
options.D: Reacts with water to form acid

questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide is colourless and odourless and interferes with oxygen transport by haemoglobin. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the key difference between an element and a compound?

options.A: An element contains one type of atom; a compound contains elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio
options.B: An element contains two types of atoms; a compound contains one type
options.C: Both contain one type of atom

questions.explanation: An element contains one type of atom; a compound contains elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio; a mixture has variable composition. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Do physical separation methods change the chemical identities of mixture components?

options.B: No, they do not normally change the chemical identities

questions.explanation: Physical separation methods do not normally change the chemical identities of mixture components. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Atomic number equals:
questions.explanation: Atomic number equals proton number; mass number equals protons plus neutrons. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Mass number equals:
questions.explanation: Mass number equals protons plus neutrons. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: In a redox reaction, what happens to oxidation and reduction?
questions.explanation: Oxidation and reduction occur together in a redox reaction. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Rusting of iron requires:
questions.explanation: Rusting of iron requires oxygen and moisture; salt can accelerate it. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Alkanes are saturated; alkenes contain:
questions.explanation: Alkanes are saturated; alkenes contain C=C; alkynes contain C≡C. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Alkynes contain:
questions.explanation: Alkynes contain C≡C; alkenes contain C=C; alkanes are saturated. This is an important exam distinction.
questions.source: Chemistry.pdf - High-yield exam cautions and distinctions

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which separation technique is used to separate ammonium chloride from a non-sublimable impurity?
questions.explanation: Sublimation can separate sublimable substances such as ammonium chloride or iodine from non-sublimable impurities.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which separation technique is used to obtain salt from seawater?
questions.explanation: Evaporation is used to obtain salt from seawater by removing the volatile solvent (water) and leaving the dissolved non-volatile solid (salt) behind.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which separation technique is used to separate dyes and pigments?
questions.explanation: Chromatography is used to separate dyes, pigments and mixtures based on different rates of movement of components between a stationary phase and a mobile phase.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which separation technique is used to separate miscible liquids with close boiling points?
questions.explanation: Fractional distillation is used to separate miscible liquids with relatively close boiling points, such as components of petroleum or liquid air.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the chemical formula of bleaching powder commonly given at school level?
